One country is counting its votes on whether copper has paid off, and the other is counting, for the first time, what has been leaving alongside it.

DR Congo – The Uranium in the Cobalt

A state that starts measuring

The Democratic Republic of Congo said on Friday it will test its cobalt exports for uranium. The decision follows research published on 30 July in the journal Nature Communications, examined by the Financial Times and Lighthouse Reports, which estimated that thousands of tonnes of the radioactive metal left the country as a by-product over roughly two decades.

Kinshasa will set up a working group, consult the International Atomic Energy Agency about a technical mission, and assess health and environmental risks within sixty days. It also plans to install radiation detectors on trucks leaving the country.

Contested, and taken seriously anyway

The government disputes the method, saying the estimates rest on modelling rather than direct measurements of exported material, and that uranium occurring alongside copper and cobalt in the region is natural and well documented. Chinese mining companies operating in the country reject the claims outright.

The head of the Congolese nuclear energy agency told the Financial Times it was technically possible and even probable that uranium had been extracted from exported ore, while stressing there is no direct evidence. The national mood is neither denial nor alarm but a wary insistence on checking, which is itself new.

Zambia – Three Days to the Copper Vote

Reform seeks its receipt

Zambians vote on Thursday for a president and parliament, with President Hakainde Hichilema seeking a second term against a fragmented opposition led by Brian Mundubile. The country is Africa’s second-largest copper producer and the world’s eighth, and copper supplies about 70% of its export earnings.

Hichilema steered the country through a punishing debt restructuring after it became the pandemic era’s first sovereign defaulter. The question this week is whether voters feel any of it in their own lives.

Stability without the receipts

The previous 1.7 billion dollar programme with the International Monetary Fund expired in January, and investors treat a successor as the real test of continuity. Standard Chartered expects this year’s deficit near 5.0% of output, more than double the government’s 2.1% target, partly because a record maize harvest obliges the state to buy heavily from farmers.

Drought has also undercut a power system that leans on hydro, forcing cuts that stall industry. Zambia’s temper is that of a country asked to be patient for five years and now being asked, politely, for proof.

South Africa – A Speech Against Violence, and Eleven Dead

Seventy years after the march

President Cyril Ramaphosa marked Women’s Day at the Union Buildings on Sunday, seventy years after thousands of women gathered there to protest against apartheid pass laws. He condemned those who try to justify abuse, saying how women dress or behave can never be an excuse.

He called on men and boys to take a stronger stand and on communities to stop turning away. He also urged more women into science and engineering.

The same weekend, in Cape Town

Eleven people were killed in three separate mass shootings in the city. Three men died in Khayelitsha, five in Langa, and three at the Barcelona settlement in Gugulethu, where two others were wounded.

Police have reinforced deployments and no arrests have been made, with motives still under investigation. The gap between the speech at the Union Buildings and the weekend in the townships is the country’s whole predicament in a single day.

Senegal – Six For, Seven Against

A candidacy that stalls at the first ballot

Former president Macky Sall took six votes in favour, seven against and two abstentions in the Security Council’s first informal ballot for United Nations secretary-general, held on 30 July. The polls are non-binding, and further rounds are expected through August and possibly into the autumn.

Two Africans are in the race, Sall and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu, who entered late. A former head of the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa judges the continent’s chances this year to be low.

A prize Africa keeps not winning

Sall was nominated by Burundi rather than by his own country, and only secured Senegal’s endorsement later. At home the ruling party still holds him responsible for deaths during protests in 2021 and 2023.

The mood in Dakar is not wounded so much as unsurprised. A continent that supplies the world’s minerals is still waiting to supply its secretary-general.

One country is counting votes on whether its copper has paid off, and its neighbour has begun counting what has been leaving alongside the same ore — the Copperbelt, at last, taking its own inventory.

Kenya – The Arithmetic of 2027

A retreat at Naivasha

President William Ruto and Oburu Odinga led a broad-based parliamentary retreat at Naivasha, gathering legislators from across the governing arrangement. The subject is the shape of the coalition heading into the 2027 election.

Kenyan politics is already organising itself around that date. Alliances are being tested well before any campaign formally begins.

Governing and campaigning at once

The country’s mood is watchful and transactional, with everyone counting numbers a year and a half early. That leaves less attention for the cost of living that drove last year’s protests.

Kenya’s economy has held up better than many of its neighbours. Its politics is the part that never rests.

Sudan – The Students Who Kept Going

Education as refusal

Sudanese students are finding ways to continue studying through a conflict that has emptied universities and scattered families. United Nations accounts describe young people sitting examinations and resuming courses in displacement.

One of them said simply that it made him dream again. It is a small sentence carrying a great deal.

What persistence is worth

A generation losing its education is the slowest and most expensive damage any conflict does. Countries that keep teaching through disaster recover years faster than those that do not.

The mood here is stubbornness rather than hope, which may be more durable. Sudan’s students are protecting the one asset nobody can carry away.

The Bigger Picture The Copperbelt is one geological formation running under two countries, and this week it holds both of the continent’s largest stories. Zambia votes on Thursday on whether five years of reform have reached ordinary lives, with copper supplying about 70% of export earnings and a deficit heading for double its target. Across the border, DR Congo has begun testing what leaves alongside the same ore, after research alleged that thousands of tonnes of uranium were exported unmeasured for two decades. The claim is disputed by the government and by the Chinese firms involved, and Kinshasa is checking anyway, which is the part that matters. Elsewhere the day was about counting of a different kind. South Africa counted eleven dead in three Cape Town shootings on the weekend its president spoke against violence, Senegal counted six votes for Macky Sall and seven against, and Kenya’s politicians counted their numbers for an election still a year and a half away. Why is DR Congo testing its cobalt exports for uranium?

What is at stake in Zambia’s election on 13 August?

Zambia is Africa’s second-largest copper producer and copper accounts for roughly 70% of export earnings, while a 1.7 billion dollar International Monetary Fund programme expired in January and Standard Chartered expects the 2026 deficit near 5.0% of output against a 2.1% target.

What did President Ramaphosa say on Women’s Day?

Speaking at the Union Buildings on Sunday 9 August, seventy years after the 1956 march against pass laws, Ramaphosa condemned those who attempt to justify abuse, saying how women dress or behave can never serve as a justification, and urged men and boys to take a stronger stand while calling on communities not to turn a blind eye. How did Macky Sall perform in the first UN straw poll?

In the Security Council’s first informal ballot on 30 July, the former Senegalese president received six votes in favour, seven against and two abstentions, a result widely read as weakening his candidacy. The polls are non-binding, with further rounds expected through August and possibly into the autumn before a single candidate is recommended to the General Assembly, and the new secretary-general takes office on 1 January 2027.

World.title: Jannik Sinner Withdraws From Cincinnati Open With Knee Injury
World.content:
World No. 1 Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from the 2026 Cincinnati Open because of a right knee injury, removing another of the tournament’s biggest stars just days before the men’s main draw begins. Sinner announced Sunday that continuing discomfort in his right knee had left him unable to compete despite treatment and work with his medical team.

“My right knee has been bothering me,” Sinner said, adding that he had to accept that he was “not ready to compete yet.” The 24-year-old Italian will instead focus on getting healthy for the US Open, which begins August 30 in New York. The withdrawal is a significant blow for Cincinnati. Sinner won the tournament in 2024 and returned to the final last year, where Carlos Alcaraz took the title after Sinner retired during the opening set.

Sinner had been expected to arrive in Ohio as the No. 1 player in the world and one of the leading favorites for the title. Instead, he joins Alcaraz among the major names missing from the men’s field. Alcaraz withdrew earlier this week because of the right wrist injury that has kept him out of competition since April.

Sinner’s absence also raises questions about how much competitive preparation he will have before the final Grand Slam of the season. He has not played since winning Wimbledon in July, where he defeated Alexander Zverev in the final to capture the fifth Grand Slam singles title of his career. Sinner had already withdrawn from the Canadian Open, meaning Cincinnati was positioned to provide his most important match preparation on North American hard courts before the US Open.

Reports from Europe in recent days had already raised doubts about his participation in Cincinnati. Sinner underwent medical examinations and treatment for the knee problem before ultimately deciding against traveling to compete. The injury does not currently appear to have changed his intention to play the US Open. Sinner made clear Sunday that preparing for New York is now the priority.

“I’m now focusing on getting ready for the US Open,” he said. Sinner’s withdrawal also changes the Cincinnati draw before play begins. Stefanos Tsitsipas, the 2022 Cincinnati finalist who had originally been listed in qualifying, is expected to move into the main field in Sinner’s place.

For Cincinnati organizers, losing both Sinner and Alcaraz removes the two players who contested last year’s championship match and two of the sport’s biggest attractions. Alexander Zverev and Novak Djokovic remain among the leading names scheduled to compete in the ATP Masters 1000 tournament.

The Cincinnati Open men’s main draw begins August 13 and runs through August 23. For Sinner, however, the immediate concern has shifted from defending ranking points or adding another Masters 1000 title to making sure his knee is ready for New York. With the US Open only three weeks away, his recovery will now be one of the biggest stories heading into the final Grand Slam of the year.

World.title: International News: Almost three-quarters of England declared in drought
World.content:
International News: Almost three-quarters of England declared in drought

By Zoila Palma: Nearly three-quarters of England has now been officially declared in drought as the country continues to experience historically dry and hot weather.

The National Drought Group said 71.3 percent of England is experiencing flash drought, with severe pressure on water resources affecting public supplies, agriculture, navigation and the environment.

The East Midlands, Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, Kent and East Sussex, and Solent and the South Downs were the latest regions placed under drought status. The North East and Yorkshire have been moved to prolonged dry weather status, the stage before drought, leaving no region in England classified as having normal water conditions.

The worsening water crisis follows provisional figures showing that England and Wales experienced their driest July since records began in 1836, with 19 English counties recording no rainfall during the entire month.

World.title: Taiwan, Belize strengthen Climate Resilience through Disaster Risk project
World.content:
Taiwan, Belize strengthen Climate Resilience through Disaster Risk project

By Zoila Palma: Taiwan and Belize are strengthening their partnership on climate resilience and disaster preparedness through initiatives aimed at improving flood monitoring and early warning systems.

In recent years, the Taiwan Technical Mission has partnered with the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change to establish nine flood monitoring stations and an early warning system covering flood-prone areas along Belize’s river basins.

Building on this mechanism, Taiwan and Belize officially launched the “Belize Multi-Hazard Risk Management Capacity Building Project” in February 2026.

The project seeks to expand Belize’s existing disaster prevention mechanisms to cover at least 70 percent of disaster-prone areas across the country.

Taiwan said it remains committed to working with Belize to strengthen the country’s capacity for disaster mitigation while reducing climate-related risks and vulnerabilities.

World.title: National Hurricane Center monitoring 3 disturbances in Atlantic
World.content:
National Hurricane Center monitoring 3 disturbances in Atlantic

By Zoila Palma: The National Hurricane Center (NHC) is monitoring three weather disturbances across the Atlantic, with one system having a 60 percent chance of developing into a tropical depression over the next seven days.

The first disturbance is located a few hundred miles south of the Cabo Verde Islands and is producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. The system is expected to move westward and merge with a tropical wave currently over West Africa. The NHC gives it a 20 percent chance of formation within 48 hours and a 60 percent chance within seven days.

A second disturbance, associated with a tropical wave in the central tropical Atlantic, is located roughly midway between West Africa and the Lesser Antilles. Some gradual development is possible through midweek as it moves westward, but unfavorable upper-level winds are expected to limit development later in the week. It has a 10 percent chance of formation over both the next 48 hours and seven days.

The third disturbance is a trough of low pressure located several hundred miles northwest of Bermuda. It is expected to move eastward north of Bermuda, with a 10 percent chance of development over the next 48 hours and seven days.

The NHC said the system is expected to reach cooler waters later this week, ending its chances of development after Wednesday.

World.title: International News: Mexico, Peru to reestablish diplomatic relations
World.content:
International News: Mexico, Peru to reestablish diplomatic relations

By Zoila Palma: Mexico and Peru will reestablish diplomatic relations following an agreement described by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum as an act of “good will” by the Peruvian government.

Sheinbaum said the decision followed Peru’s granting of safe passage to Chávez, which she described as a gesture toward Mexico.

“With this [act of good will], relations with Peru are going to be reestablished,” Sheinbaum said during her Friday morning press conference, Mexico News daily reported.

Sheinbaum also reiterated Mexico’s support for former Peruvian President Pedro Castillo, whose 2022 removal from office she has previously described as a “coup.” She said Peru’s new government is aware that Mexico will continue defending Castillo.

World.title: BCWU says 84% of members no longer support BTL’s proposed acquisition of SMART
World.content:
BCWU says 84% of members no longer support BTL’s proposed acquisition of SMART

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Belize Communications Workers’ Union (BCWU) says an overwhelming majority of its members have withdrawn their support for Belize Telemedia Limited’s proposed acquisition of Speednet Communications Limited, the company which operates SMART.

In a press release issued on Monday, August 10, the union said that following an emergency membership meeting on August 6, 84 percent of its members indicated that they no longer support the acquisition as it is currently proposed.

According to the BCWU, members had initially supported the acquisition during a BTL employee town hall on January 22, but only on the “express understanding” that concerns raised by the union would be adequately addressed. Those concerns included job security for existing BTL employees, the financial implications of the transaction, governance and disclosure issues, the integration of SMART employees, and whether those workers would be able to join the BCWU.

The union said it had also sought assurances that any acquisition would be conducted through a phased process with meaningful consultation involving the National Trade Union Congress of Belize (NTUCB). The BCWU says discussions continued with BTL management, but members remain concerned about what they consider insufficient information and consultation surrounding the proposed deal.

The development comes days after BTL’s Board of Directors approved management’s proposal to acquire 100 percent of Speednet’s issued share capital. BTL has placed the proposed investment at approximately $80 million, while stressing that the transaction is not yet final and remains subject to continued due diligence, negotiations and final approval of a Share Purchase Agreement. BTL has also said the transaction would not require additional borrowing or funding from the Social Security Board.

BTL has maintained that acquiring Speednet could reduce duplication of telecommunications infrastructure, improve reliability, expand connectivity and allow greater investment in underserved areas. Earlier this year, the company also told the public that job protection, current pricing and regulatory compliance were among the issues being considered as part of the proposed transaction.

The proposal has faced sustained scrutiny from unions and the business community. The Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry has called for the process to be halted pending greater financial disclosure and safeguards for competition, warning about the implications of bringing the country’s two major telecommunications providers under one ownership structure.

The BCWU says it will now align itself with the NTUCB in determining its next steps, insisting that BTL employees are stakeholders in the process and that their voices must be heard.

World.title: Smart opens new showroom in Caye Caulker
World.content:
Smart opens new showroom in Caye Caulker

By Zoila Palma: Smart officially opened its new showroom in Caye Caulker today offering residents and visitors access to Smart’s telecommunications services and special grand opening promotions.

The new showroom is located on Calle del Sol and features special offers to mark the opening, including a free SIM card for the first 10 customers.

Customers can also take advantage of Smart’s “Double Up or Triple Up” promotion, receiving double credit on purchases from $1 to $29.99 and triple credit on purchases of $30 or more.

The new showroom provides Caye Caulker residents with a convenient location to access Smart services and stay connected.

World.title: International News: 20 dead as 7.4-magnitude earthquake shakes Colombia
World.content:
International News: 20 dead as 7.4-magnitude earthquake shakes Colombia

By Zoila Palma: At least 20 people have been killed and dozens of buildings collapsed after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia today.

The quake trapped residents under debris, injured others and forced people to evacuate their homes, with tremors felt as far away as the capital, Bogotá, AP reports.

The U.S. Geological Survey and Colombia’s Geological Service said the earthquake was centered near San José del Palmar in the Chocó region, about 400 kilometers west of Bogotá, at a depth of approximately 107 kilometers. The quake was also felt in neighboring Ecuador and was followed by aftershocks measuring 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude.

Colombia’s Geological Service described the earthquake as the strongest recorded in the country in the past decade.

World.title: Mayor Jorge Rosales, Jenny Martinez set for PUP convention showdown
World.content:
Mayor Jorge Rosales, Jenny Martinez set for PUP convention showdown

By Zoila Palma: The People’s United Party (PUP) is scheduled to host a convention on August 23, 2026 to elect its municipal Mayoral and councilor candidates in Benque Viejo.

Two-term Mayor Jorge Rosales will face Jenny Martinez.

“This convention is an opportunity to demonstrate that together, we are stronger. As a team, we share the same commitment: to serve with respect and dedication, always putting the interests of our community above personal interests,” Martinez said.

Mayor Rosales has served as Mayor of Benque Viejo del Carmen since 2020 and his leadership marked a new chapter focused on community leadership and addressing the needs of local residents through municipal service and development initiatives.

“We extend a warm greeting and invitation to each and every one of you to come out and cast your vote of confidence for the continued development and transformation of our beautiful town. With plans different from what we’ve seen before, and with a brighter future for everyone—I said everyone. This August 23rd, come out and make the right decision. Team Rosales and your Mayor, Jorge Rosales, are here. The decision is yours,” Rosales expressed.

Residents will also elect 6 candidates to represent the PUP in the upcoming municipal elections.

Council member candidates include:

World.title: Tropical depression could form in Atlantic by the end of the week
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is advising that a tropical depression could form in the Atlantic during the latter half of this week.

The NOAA says an area of low pressure located a few hundred miles south of the Cabo Verde Islands is producing disorganised showers and thunderstorms.

As this system moves slowly westward, a tropical wave currently over west Africa is expected to merge with it in a couple of days.

Environmental conditions are forecast to be more conducive for development by midweek, and a tropical depression could form during the latter half of this week while the system moves westward to west-northwestward across the central tropical Atlantic.

Formation chance through 48 hours is low at 20 per cent but formation chance through seven days is medium at 60 per cent.

World.title: Bold Bruce
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding

NEW YORK, USA — Former Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding has earned the backing of many within the Diaspora community here for what is being described as his “bold, factual and truthful position” on the souring relationship between Jamaica and America, two staunch allies.



Speaking in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania last week, Golding expressed hopes that “the United States will soften the tone of its relationship with Jamaica and rekindle the strong, decades-old bond between both nations which Jamaicans cherish.

Saying that current demands by Washington are “at odds with the very essence of true friendship”, he pointed to the many challenges facing the island as established rules are being discarded and “new rules are being handed down, not after discussions and negotiations, but unilaterally by social media postings at 2:30 in the morning when most of us are asleep”.

The former Jamaican leader, who stepped away in 2011 and handed over the reins to now Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, was addressing the annual Team Jamaica Bickle Independence Gala on Emancipation Day, August 1, 2026.

The gala celebrated Jamaica’s 64th anniversary of Independence and raised funds in support of Jamaican and other Caribbean athletes’ participation in the yearly Penn Relays in the US, a must-stop on the annual sports calendar for speedy Jamaican high school students.

Golding appeared to be voicing sentiments many Jamaicans in his US audience feel but could not express themselves. Some murmured among themselves that he must not fear losing his US visa.

Called to ask his view Sunday, Golding said he did not wish to trivialise the matter and he had said enough on the subject.

But reacting to the former prime minister’s assessment of the bilateral relations, Stafford Grant, founder and president of the US-based Jamaica Ex-Service Men and Women Foundation, said after the speech:

“Golding didn’t just give a speech, he gave Jamaica a masterclass in geopolitical survival. His address laid bare the brutal reality of being a small island nation caught in the cross hairs of superpower diplomacy.

“The former prime minister’s speech should serve as a profound wake-up call for every Jamaican. His vocal defence is more critical than ever, and I trust Jamaicans will understand that international diplomacy is shifting from collaborative negotiations to unilateral madness,” Grant declared.

Raymond Rhoden, a Florida-based retired adjunct professor, described Golding’s stance as “bold, principled, factual and diplomatic”, adding that he believes Jamaica needs to stand up and take a principled position on the current situation.

Irwine Clare Sr, co-founder of Team Jamaica Bickle, said the issues raised by the former head of government were “pungent, timely, and well articulated on behalf of the voiceless and those who have avoided the conversation due to fear of reprisal or just being downright spineless”.

“This speech must also be placed in context, because clearly he [Golding] recognises the agonising situation that Caribbean leaders find themselves in, especially against the backdrop that they do not speak from a united perspective,” said Clare Sr.

In his address, which was punctuated by applause, Golding spoke of the discontinuation of the Cuban medical mission programme, America’s fierce opposition to China’s investments in Jamaica, and the highly controversial third-country nationals arrangements between the US and a number of Caribbean countries, as examples of actions that run counter to harmonious relations.

“True friends don’t abuse your friendship; they don’t make unreasonable demands of you. They should be there to help you. Holding a gun at your head and insisting that you must be reasonable and do things their way is not friendship,” Golding suggested.

“The United States has put us under severe stress, and that’s not what friends are for,” he said, pointing to the damage the Jamaican economy could suffer should Jamaica stand up and try to fight back.

“There are many at home and abroad who are outraged at what is taking place, who are incensed at what is being meted out to us, who are angry that we have not pushed back, that we haven’t stood up like President Lula da Silva of Brazil who declared that, ‘Brazil’s destiny is for Brazilians alone to determine — without foreign interference or otherwise.’ “

Noting that Brazil is large and provides a US$57-billion market for American exports, Golding warned that little Jamaica is not in that league, struggling to find markets for its own goods.

“With the US market accounting for half our total exports, if our exports to the US market were slapped with a 50 per cent tariff our manufacturing sector would fall apart and thousands of persons would lose their jobs,” said Golding.

Agreeing with Golding, Dr Rupert Francis, who heads the Jamaica Diaspora Task Force on Crime Intervention and Prevention, argued that “we need to get back to the more amiable friendship we had with the United States for many years”.

University lecturer Dr Allan Cunningham said Golding’s speech focused on what he describes as the “hypocrisy of the rules-based order”, noting that “the speech acts as a call for regional realism — that without a unified foreign policy Caribbean states remain vulnerable to US cowboy diplomacy”.

World.title: Public funds not enough for climate resilience — Samuda
World.content:
Matthew Samuda, minister of water, environment and climate change, delivers the keynote address at National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited’s inaugural Corporate Insights Breakfast. Addressing business leaders, Samuda underscored the importance of public-private collaboration in strengthening Jamaica’s climate resilience and preparing businesses, communities and the wider economy for the growing risks associated with climate change..

MINISTER of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is arguing that Jamaica cannot rely on public funds alone to build the infrastructure and systems needed to withstand the growing effects of climate change.

Samuda said greater participation will be required from private investors, financial institutions, and international partners as the country seeks to strengthen critical infrastructure and improve its ability to recover from climate-related disruptions.

“Public funds are simply not enough to address the challenges posed by climate change. We need financing from all available sources — including public, private, domestic and international partners — if we are to successfully transition to climate resilience,” Samuda said.

He was speaking at the inaugural NCB Corporate Breakfast Series, hosted by National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), which brought together policymakers, business leaders and financial sector representatives to discuss climate resilience, infrastructure, and investment.

Samuda said strengthening Jamaica’s resilience will require cooperation across the public and private sectors as the country responds to the increasing threat posed by extreme weather and other climate-related events.

The issue has taken on greater significance as disruptions to electricity, water, telecommunications, transportation and other critical services can have wide-ranging effects on households, communities and businesses.

NCBJ Interim Chief Executive Officer Sheree Martin said the changing environment also requires organisations to rethink how they prepare for and respond to disruptions.

“Strategy sharpens in conversation, not in isolation, and capital works best when it is guided by an honest read on where a business is heading,” Martin said.

She said access to financing, strong partnerships, and informed decision-making will become increasingly important as organisations adjust to economic and structural changes.

“As businesses adapt to changing realities, access to informed perspectives, strong partnerships, and the right financial solutions become increasingly important,” Martin said.

Hugh Graham, director of Paramount Industries, said businesses also have a responsibility to prepare for disruptions and protect their operations and employees.

“For businesses, resilience is about being able to keep operating, protect jobs, and continue serving customers when disruption occurs,” Graham said.

“That requires investment and preparation at the company level, but it also requires strong infrastructure, sound policy,and access to financing.” Graham said closer coordination among Government, financial institutions, and businesses could improve Jamaica’s ability to withstand shocks and recover more quickly. “The more Government, financial institutions, and businesses can plan together, the better positioned we will be to withstand shocks and recover more quickly,” he said. NCB said the breakfast series is intended to bring together policymakers, business leaders, and other stakeholders to discuss issues affecting Jamaica’s economic development and long-term sustainability.

World.title: Missing Oliver Mair: Miami’s loss is New York’s gain
World.content:
Consul General Oliver Mair (in cap) waiting to receive the key to the South Florida City of Lauderhill from Jamaican-born Mayor Denise Grant on Saturday night at the 64th anniversary of Jamaica’s Independence celebrations staged at the Lauderhill Performing Arts Centre. With them are city commissioners out to support the Jamaican event.

THE end of an era.



That is what many Diasporans, including top Jamaican American attorney Alison Smith, are calling the relocation of Consul General Oliver Mair from the Jamaican Consulate in Miami to the Jamaican Consulate in New York.

Mair, who served in his role in Miami for over seven years, and was responsible for overseeing 13 states, now moves to the New York post where he will serve Jamaica’s largest overseas population.

Smith, the first woman of colour to ever lead the Broward County Bar Association, in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, first met Mair while serving in her role as president of the Bar. In fact, she says, her first official engagement as president of the Bar was to visit the Jamaican Consulate in Miami to discuss potential ways to advance the interests of the Diaspora through collaborative work with the consulate.

“Over the years that I have either collaborated with CG, as he is affectionately called, or attended one of the many events he has hosted to promote Jamaican culture, I have seen CG’s uncanny ability to connect to people and make them feel seen, heard and respected,” the attorney said.

“Not many people can do that. He is charismatic, warm, receptive, kind, and simply the type of ambassador every country would want representing them. His absence will leave a gaping hole that a very big presence will need to fill.”

Copious praises have been heaped on Mair, a Campion College old boy, since his promotion was announced by Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith. He has been lauded by many Diasporans who are excited and expectant as it relates to Mair’s new position.

Suzette Lloyd, the chief representative officer in Florida of the Victoria Mutual Building Society (VMBS), stated: “CG Mair’s appointment to New York reflects his proven leadership and unwavering commitment to Jamaica’s Diaspora; the VM Group looks forward to continued collaboration as he brings his Miami-honed diplomatic strengths to this important new role.”

Janice McIntosh, member of the Jamaica Global Diaspora Council for the Southern United States, noted that, “Consul General Oliver Mair transformed the role into one that was not only highly visible but deeply connected to the Jamaican community, inspiring unprecedented engagement and participation across South Florida and the 13 Southern states.”

“Through his energetic, approachable leadership and unwavering commitment to service, he has united the Diaspora, strengthened community partnerships, and left a lasting impact that extends well beyond the walls of the consulate,” said McIntosh.

If his time in Miami is any indication, Diasporans in New York will greatly benefit from his appointment.

As attorney Marlon Hill, who worked closely with Mair on many projects over the years, put it: “New York is the beneficiary of an unrestrained advocate for Jamaican excellence and community impact. Mek sure seh the music is cued up because this CG always has a tune to play!” — a reference to the CG’s love for promoting Jamaican music and culture.

World.title: High marks for Redeemed: A Father’s Love at première
World.content:
Executive Producer Rev Dr Otis Manning (left) and gospel recording artiste Kevin Downswell at the première of Redeemed: A Father’s Love held at Carib 5 on Monday. Garfield Robinson

Carib 5 cinema in Kingston was the epicentre of laughter, gasps, cheers, and spontaneous outbursts on Monday night as audiences reacted to the twists, turns, and emotional moments of Redeemed: A Father’s Love at its official Jamaican première.

The faith-based crime drama, which blends suspense, family, faith, and redemption, drew a diverse audience for the red carpet affair, with members of the cast and supporting individuals stepping out in snazzy pieces for the occasion.

The première also attracted strong support from several church communities, reflecting the film’s faith-based foundation. Among those in attendance were gospel entertainers Kevin Downswell and Petra Kaye, who joined members of the cast, production team, and other guests for the screening.

For Executive Producer Reverend Dr Otis Manning, the warm reception from the audience was among the most rewarding aspects of bringing the project to the big screen.

“I’m grateful. I’m thankful. Everything turned out well. The most exciting thing is that people are loving it. I’ve loved it, but, it’s more exciting to watch people loving what you’ve done,” Manning told the Jamaica Observer at the première.

Redeemed: A Father’s Love follows the devastating aftermath of a childhood kidnapping, as long-buried secrets begin to surface and dangerous truths threaten to unravel the lives of those involved. Through its exploration of betrayal, identity, forgiveness, and unconditional love, the film challenges audiences to confront difficult questions about truth, family, and redemption.

Leading the cast is acclaimed American actor Malik Yoba, whose commanding performance anchors the emotionally charged narrative. He is joined by an accomplished ensemble including Co-producer Jacinth Headlam, veteran actor Cornelius Grant, social media personality Julie Mango, gospel dancehall singjay Prince Saj, Justin Awn, and entertainer Safaree Samuels, whose recent public declaration of faith has drawn renewed attention to his appearance in the film.

Although faith is at the heart of the production, Manning and the film-makers are clear that Redeemed: A Father’s Love is not intended solely for Christian audiences. The film’s themes of broken families, lost identity, forgiveness, unconditional love and the hope of restoration are presented as universal experiences that can resonate across cultures, geographical boundaries, and religious backgrounds.

For Manning, the film’s ability to affect people on a personal level is perhaps its greatest achievement.

“The best part of the film was listening to testimonies. A veteran in the business, Chris Browne told me that he’d shot movies for 40 years and there is nothing he would’ve changed,” he said.

Manning also recalled an experience involving one of the film’s actors, who came to a personal realisation while working on the production.

“I was also doing an interview with one of the actors, on set, and he said while we were filming the movie taught him that there were some stuff he had in his heart that he had to forgive. It was on the movie set, while doing the role, that he realised, ‘I messed up.’ That was awesome; to know that my movie is really helping people. I am hoping that it will have the same effect on other viewers,” he said.

Manning shared that

Redeemed: A Father’s Love marks his foray into film-making. He said the idea of making a movie had been on his mind for some time, but he waited until he felt ready to pursue it.

“I knew I wanted to do a movie, but I wasn’t ready for it. When I was ready, I met somebody who was an actress and I left it hanging for a year. When I called her, she explained that she’s done films before. She came down and she literally walked me through. So, big up to Jacinth Headlam. She literally taught me what to do, and how to. She and I did the screening for the actors and everything. Sometimes I had to pull up my socks very hard, but I’m grateful that she really gave me the balance,” Manning said.

Attendees were left in awe following Monday’s viewing.

“I absolutely loved it. It had everything that I look for in a great film; the suspense, the drama, the humour and, most importantly, a powerful message. I found myself laughing one minute and sitting on the edge of my seat the next. It was really well done, and I think a lot of people will be able to relate to the story,” one viewer told the Observer.

Manning added that the film was produced out of pocket through the support of the church community, but believes greater investment is needed to propel Jamaica’s film industry forward.

He is calling for increased support from both the Government and the private sector, arguing that local film-makers need more resources and opportunities to develop and produce quality content.

World.title: ATL Automotive driven to succeed — now in 21 Caribbean territories
World.content:
Guyanese President Dr Mohamed Irfaan Ali (front row, second left) and executive chairman of Sandals and ATL groups Adam Stewart (front row, second right) move towards the launch event for Cam Motors Inc, accompanied by Rakesh Puri (left), chairman of Continental Group of Companies and director, CAM Motors ; Dr Ashni Singh (right), senior minister within the Ministry of Finance of Guyana; and Vishok Persaud (immediately behind the president), CEO of ENet Inc and director of CAM Motors Inc.

One doesn’t have to be a motor vehicle enthusiast to feel the pride and joy of Jamaicans who have witnessed the relentless speed of the evolution of ATL Automotive into a Caribbean hub, covering 21 countries and territories stretching from Bermuda in the north to Panama in Central America.

From its one iconic Honda brand, the Caribbean hub has expanded outwards from the Jamaican capital, Kingston, to become the regional distribution, dealer development and support division of ATL Automotive Group, the region’s largest and most diverse of its kind.

The hub acts as the central link between international automotive manufacturers and dealer partners across the Caribbean and surrounding markets. It provides the infrastructure, expertise and hands-on support required to successfully introduce, operate and grow global automotive brands across what is a complex region.

With a portfolio boasting an impressive array of the hottest deals on wheels, like BMW, MINI, BYD, Foton, MG, Omoda & Jaecoo, and Jetour, brand representation varies by market, with each franchise placed according to the opportunities, customer requirements and strength of the local dealer partner.

And although ATL Automotive began with one brand, operating from one dealership in Kingston, the ambition was always bigger — an automotive network with the scale, expertise and infrastructure required to give customers across the region greater choice, stronger support and better representation from global manufacturers.

Mission accomplished.

Across the 21 countries and territories, ATL Automotive now works through approximately 35 dealer operations, having grown itself into a position to deliver a level of automotive choice and regional support unmatched in the Caribbean. It’s a story Jamaica has seen before. “During the 1990s, Sandals demonstrated that a Jamaican company could successfully expand across the Caribbean by respecting the individuality of each destination while building the strength of a regional brand,” says Executive Chairman Adam Stewart.

In the 1980s, Sandals Resorts grew from a single Jamaican property into the country’s most successful home-grown international superbrand. It achieved that growth by recognising the wider potential of the Caribbean, building scale across multiple markets and combining strong regional knowledge with international standards.

A car enthusiast of some renown himself, Stewart notes that the approach taken in the automotive industry is a replication of the resort brand that pulls the world to the Caribbean. “We don’t try to make the Caribbean fit one model; we build solutions that recognise the uniqueness of every market while harnessing the collective strength of the region,” he recounts.

“By bringing markets together, ATL is able to create stronger purchasing power, more competitive pricing, improved warranty support, greater access to technical expertise, more consistent retail standards and stronger representation from manufacturers,” Stewart is now showing off.

He drives home a key point: ATL gives Caribbean customers access to more brands, more vehicle types and more mobility solutions than individual markets could easily secure on their own.

“The goal is not simply to sell more vehicles or collect more brands. It is to build a connected regional platform that gives manufacturers a credible route into the Caribbean, gives dealers access to world-class support and gives customers more choice, better service and greater confidence,” explains CEO Patrick Wilson.

Wilson suggests that for their manufacturing partners, the value is clear. Instead of managing relationships across dozens of individual dealerships, they have one trusted regional partner with the experience, capability and governance to deliver consistently high standards across multiple markets.

“Our leadership team brings decades of automotive and commercial experience, allowing manufacturers to focus on strategy while we manage the complexity of execution across the Caribbean,” says Wilson.

The road from ATL Automotive to Caribbean hub has been eventful. ATL Automotive was awarded the regional master dealership for BMW and MINI in November 2015 — a big deal for a small country — getting the operation on the road in Jamaica in April 2016, with capacity to provide regional support to eight Caribbean markets.

Next came BYD and the subsequent introduction of further passenger, commercial and new-energy vehicle brands. Today, the hub represents seven international automotive brands across the 21 countries and territories, reflecting significant growth in both geographic reach and the breadth of its automotive portfolio.

The ATL Automotive Caribbean Hub currently operates across Antigua and Barbuda; Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao; The Bahamas; Barbados; Belize; Bermuda; the British Virgin Islands; the Cayman Islands; Grenada; Guyana; Haiti; Panama; St Lucia; St Martin; St Vincent and the Grenadines; Suriname; Trinidad and Tobago; the Turks and Caicos Islands; and Jamaica.

Not every brand, Wilson notes, is represented in every market. The hub works with manufacturers and local dealer partners to determine the most appropriate brand and product opportunities for each territory.

“For example, Jetour is represented regionally but is not currently represented by ATL in Jamaica, while MG is among the brands represented in Haiti,” he says, adding that ATL Automotive also represents Honda, Kia, Audi, Volkswagen, and Porsche in Jamaica but they are not currently managed regionally through the Caribbean hub.

The centralised structure of the hub enables international manufacturers to work through one experienced regional organisation while maintaining strong, locally operated dealer businesses in each territory.

A central part of the role is the development of people through a dedicated training centre in Kingston, providing hands-on training for dealer personnel from across the region. Training includes sales, product knowledge, after sales operations, technical diagnosis, service procedures, warranty management and high-voltage systems for electric and hybrid vehicles.

The Kingston-based training operation helps ensure that dealer teams across the network are equipped to meet the technical, operational and customer-service standards required by each manufacturer.

For the hub, a thing of pride is its specialist “Flying Doctor” service for dealer partners facing technical matters that cannot be resolved locally. Senior technical specialists can be deployed to regional markets to support diagnosis, repair and complex technical cases.

This service gives dealers access to advanced technical expertise without requiring each individual market to independently maintain every level of specialist capability.

Under a dedicated regional marketing operation out of Jamaica, the team works alongside manufacturers and dealer partners to plan and execute campaigns suited to individual markets while maintaining the global standards and identity of each brand.

Support can include regional campaign development, digital marketing, social media, public relations, product launches, lead generation, creative execution, and dealer-level marketing activity.

Most dealer operations within the hub network are independently owned local businesses, all working closely to benefit from the brand access, training, technical expertise, operational standards and marketing support needed to build strong and sustainable businesses.

Wilson pointed to the two regional joint ventures — Guyana — CAM Motors — an automotive operation supporting ATL-represented brands in Guyana; and Trinidad and Tobago — Spectra Motors and LAFAST Motors — supporting ATL-represented brands in Trinidad and Tobago.

“Our customers remain our most important concern and the hub helps to ensure that vehicles are backed by trained teams, recognised retail standards, manufacturer-supported warranty processes and consistent after-sales care,” Wilson emphasises.

Executive Chairman Stewart explains the vision:

“Many people look at the Caribbean and see one region. We see distinct markets, each with its own culture, economy, currency, regulations and way of doing business. That understanding has been built over decades, and it’s what makes the ATL Automotive Caribbean hub so powerful.

“By connecting these economies under one umbrella, we’re creating greater scale, stronger partnerships, better support for our dealer network and new opportunities for global automotive brands. It’s a model that benefits everyone — our manufacturers, our dealer partners, our Jamaican-based regional team and, ultimately, the customers we all serve.

“It’s proof that world-class regional businesses can be built from Jamaica, creating value not only for our company but for the wider Caribbean economy.”

In sum, according to Wilson, the hub works alongside its dealer partners, supporting where they need it most, sharing best practice and providing additional resources that help them grow while always respecting that they know their local market best.

“We do the hard work behind the scenes, ensuring every brand is represented to the highest standard in every market,” says Wilson, unable to hide his passion for the job.

World.title: Who should get the Reggae Icon Award?
World.content:
Bob Marley, the Third World’s biggest reggae megastar

At last Thursday’s Independence Grand Gala, Busy Signal and Wayne Wonder joined Sizzla Kalonji, Capleton, Beres Hammond, Leroy Sibbles, Derrick Morgan, Rita Marley, Morgan Heritage, Third World, Ken Boothe, Toots Hibbert, Dawn Penn, Melody Makers, Byron Lee and the Dragonnaires, Shaggy, Grub Cooper, and Sanchez, as recipients of the culture ministry’s Reggae Icon Award.



In this article shared with the Jamaica Observer, Dr Leo Gilling, criminologist, Diaspora strategist, journalist, philanthropist and policy analyst, questions what exactly does the award measure and why a slew of apparently deserving artistes were leapfrogged by some of the current recipients.

Following is part one of a lightly edited version of the article:

Let me begin with what this article is not.

This is not an argument that Sanchez, Wayne Wonder, Busy Signal, Sizzla Kalonji, Capleton, Beres Hammond, Leroy Sibbles, Derrick Morgan, Rita Marley, Morgan Heritage, or Third World et al are undeserving of national recognition.

They are accomplished artistes who have made significant contributions to Jamaican music. My question is different.

If Jamaica has established qualifications for determining who should receive the Reggae Icon Award, do those qualifications adequately explain who is selected — and, just as importantly, who is selected first? That distinction matters.

An award does more than recognise achievement. A national award helps establish a standard. It tells younger artistes, the music industry, Jamaicans and the wider world: This is what we mean when we call someone a Jamaican music icon.

If Jamaica creates a national award intended to represent the highest standard of musical excellence, then the first recipients should help define that standard. The pioneers should establish the benchmark.

Subsequent generations should have something meaningful toward which to aspire. If you create a benchmark, you should begin with the benchmark.

The five qualifications

The qualifications publicly associated with selection for the Reggae Icon Award can be summarised in five broad areas:

1. Pioneering Foundation & Evolution

The artiste should have played a foundational role in originating, developing, or evolving Jamaican genres such as ska, rocksteady, reggae, dancehall, or dub.

2. Authenticity & Conscious Message

The artiste’s work should demonstrate cultural grounding, positive or uplifting messages, social consciousness, spirituality, national pride, or advocacy for social justice.

3. Global Ambassadorship

The artiste should demonstrate sustained international impact and help expand the global footprint of Jamaican music.

4. Longevity & Artistic Consistency

The artiste should demonstrate decades of artistic excellence, influential recordings and resonance across generations.

5. Community & Nation-Building Impact

Consideration is also given to mentorship, charitable activity, youth development and other contributions to Jamaican communities.

At first glance, these appear to be reasonable qualifications. But something interesting happens when we actually apply them.

For purposes of analysis, I assigned each qualification a maximum of 10 points, producing a possible total of 50.

These are not Government of Jamaica scores. They are my analytical application of the qualifications and are intended to encourage discussion about how the criteria operate when applied consistently.

Artiste Pioneer / Evolution Cultural / Conscious Global Longevity Community Total /50

Rita Marley – 9 10 10 9 10 48

Leroy Sibbles – 10 9 9 10 8 46

Beres Hammond – 8 9 10 10 9 46

Derrick Morgan – 10 8 9 10 8 45

Sizzla Kalonji – 8 10 9 9 9 45

Capleton – 8 10 9 9 8 44

Peetah Morgan / Morgan Heritage – 8 9 10 9 8 44

AJ Brown / Third World – 7 9 10 9 7 42

Busy Signal – 8 8 8 8 7 39

Sanchez – 4 7 8 10 7 36

Wayne Wonder – 6 6 9 9 6 36

Reasonable people will disagree with individual scores. That is expected. But the numbers themselves are not the central argument. They simply force us to examine what the qualifications actually mean.

When viewed against those qualifications, the pattern of selections can appear erratic and inconsistent, particularly when artistes with demonstrably stronger claims to pioneering influence, historical importance and global impact remain outside the list.

And perhaps nowhere is the difficulty clearer than with the word “pioneering”. What exactly is a pioneer?

A pioneer is not simply someone who became successful, popular, or enduring. A pioneer changes the architecture of the music; introduces something; transforms something; opens a previously closed door, or creates an approach upon which subsequent generations build.

That distinction matters because if “pioneering” is one of the measures of icon status, it cannot simply become another word for longevity or popularity.

Derrick Morgan has a genuine pioneering claim because his career reaches into the formative development of ska, rocksteady and reggae.

Leroy Sibbles has one because his work as vocalist, musician and arranger intersects directly with the development of Jamaica’s early reggae sound.

But consider Sanchez.

Sanchez is unquestionably one of Jamaica’s great vocalists. His voice is distinctive. His longevity is extraordinary. Generations of Jamaicans know his recordings. But a substantial part of his career has involved interpreting songs written and previously recorded by others.

That is an artistic accomplishment. It can even be an extraordinary artistic accomplishment. But it is not necessarily pioneering. If pioneering means originating, developing, or substantially evolving Jamaican music, longevity cannot simply be substituted for innovation.

The same question arises, although differently, with Wayne Wonder.

Wayne Wonder became an important participant in modern dancehall and reggae crossover and achieved significant international success. But was he a pioneer of that evolution, or an exceptionally successful participant within it? Those are not the same things.

This distinction is important because otherwise every successful artiste eventually becomes a “pioneer”. That empties the word of meaning.

A great singer can be an icon without being a pioneer. A great songwriter can be an icon without being an international superstar. An artiste can revolutionise Jamaican music without operating a charitable foundation. And an artiste can achieve enormous international commercial success without having created a new musical form. These are different kinds of achievement. A credible national recognition system should be capable of distinguishing among them.

The historical question

Now consider something else.

The Reggae Icon Award was introduced in 2019. Reggae was not. Neither was Jamaican popular music. By the time this award was created, Jamaica already possessed more than half a century of extraordinary musical history. There was therefore already a historical backlog of giants.

Artistes had helped create ska. Others had shaped rocksteady.

Others had helped create reggae. Some revolutionised the Jamaican deejay tradition. Others developed dub. Others helped establish dancehall.

Some carried these musical forms around the world. Others influenced musical genres far beyond Jamaica. So when Jamaica established a new national award bearing the word “Icon”, there was an important question to answer from the beginning: Who establishes the benchmark?

If the qualifications emphasise pioneering, longevity, international impact, cultural authenticity and national contribution, one would reasonably expect the earliest recipients to include the artistes whose careers most completely embody those qualities.

This is why the sequence matters. It is not enough to ask whether an individual recipient qualifies. We must also ask: Who else qualifies more strongly? And: Why did one qualifying artiste receive recognition before another?

Those questions do not diminish anyone who has already received the award. They test the integrity of the selection architecture.

The fairest way to examine this is simple. Take exactly the same qualifications. Do not change them. Do not create special rules for anyone. Apply them to Jamaican-born artistes who have not received the award.

What happens when Bob Marley, Toots Hibbert, Jimmy Cliff, Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Burning Spear, Marcia Griffiths, Dennis Brown, U-Roy, Gregory Isaacs, Shabba Ranks, Ini Kamoze, Eek-A-Mouse, and others are placed beside the existing recipients?

If the qualifications are sound, they should help us understand the hierarchy. If they cannot, perhaps the problem is not the artistes. Perhaps the problem is the criteria.

That is where Part II begins.

Tomorrow: Jamaica’s Reggae Icon Award – when the same test is applied to the giants

World.title: GOLDEN GIRLS
World.content:
Members of Jamaica’s women’s 4x100m relay team (from left) Natrece East, Sashana Johnson, Shanoya Douglas, and Thieana-Lee Terrelonge celebrate after winning the gold medal on Sunday’s final day of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. The team ran a World Under-20-leading 42.89 seconds, the fourth-fastest time ever in the age group. (Photo: Paul Reid)Paul Reid

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s fourth-consecutive women’s 4x100m relay gold medal delivered a special moment for double silver medallist Shanoya Douglas on more than one levels, as the island closed out the World Athletics Under-20 Championships in strong fashion at Hayward Field, Eugene, Oregon, on Sunday.

The team ran 42.89 seconds – the fourth fastest in history among Under-20 women – to give Jamaica three of the top-four times ever.

Jamaica won an additional three medals on Sunday’s final day, a gold and two bronze, with Joseph Salmon in the men’s discus and the men’s 4x100m team both finishing third, for a total of eight medals at the championship — two gold, three silver and three bronze, to finish fourth on the medal table.

Douglas, who anchored the team to a World Under-20 leading 42.89 seconds, was part of back-to-back gold medal-winning teams, after her role in Lima, Peru, last year, told the Jamaica Observer, “The gold really means a lot for me because I wanted to continue the streak to four straight. This is what we are know for, winning gold medals in relays and it meant a lot to be able to continue that streak.”

Douglas, who came into the championships as the world leader and favourite in the 100m and 200m, was upstaged by American Mia Maxwell in both finals and after a quick reflection, hinted at her disappointment having not topped the podium in the individual event, “knowing that I’d broke the streak in the 100m,” she said.

She was part of two changes to the team that ran in the semi-finals. Along with lead-off runner Sashana Johnson and powered by strong legs from Theianna-Lee Terrelonge and Natrece East on the second and third legs, Jamaica held off Switzerland, who took the silver in 43.36 seconds and Belgium, who ran a national under-20 record 43.91 seconds for third.

With 100m silver medallist Gary Card and Nyrone Wade back from the winning team two years ago, the men’s team finished third in 39.01 seconds with Kyle Bodden leading off and Sanjay Seymore on anchor.

The USA, with men’s sprint double champion Tate Taylor on anchor, ran a Under-20 world record 38.16 seconds to take the gold, with Great Britain second with an Area Under-20 record 38.90 seconds.

There was drama in the men’s discus throw final with the lead changing hands no fewer then six times in the final two rounds, which saw the Jamaicans, Salmon and Kamari Kennedy, move into the first two spots before dropping to fifth and sixth places.

When the smoke settled, Salmon, the world leader, was third with 64.37m and Kennedy fourth with a massive new personal best of 64.18m, which also sees him ranked fourth in the world.

American Simon Rosselli won with a national Under-20 record of 66.39m coming into the final round with Estonia’s Sten-Erik Iir taking silver with a personal best 65.42m, also in the final round.

Jahvanie Tyrell was eighth in the men’s 400m hurdles with 53.23 seconds, after running a lifetime best 49.98 seconds in the semifinals on Saturday.

Shevaughn Thomas failed to finish the women’s 400m hurdles final.

Both 4x400m relay teams also finished down the track. The women’s team of Daniellia Dixon, Kristen Herbert, Davine Dickenson and Kevongaye Fowler were sixth in 3:34.28, while the men’s team of Nishawn Walker, Jabari Matheson, Jason Pitter and Jabulani McLeod were fifth in 3:05.71 seconds.

World.title: UK approves its second weight-loss pill while EU access lags
World.content:
However, with the arrival of the first GLP-1 pill Wegovy (semaglutide) from Danish competitor Novo Nordisk — which launched in the U.S. and U.K. this year and is soon expected in some EU countries — demand for the more-convenient tablet is expected to rise.

Novo Nordisk has been attempting to reach as many patients as possible with its pill to capture market share, said CEO Mike Doustdar last week.

Doustdar also said the company would soon launch in Germany at its chosen price, ignoring pressure from the U.S. administration to raise prices in Europe.

Washington has been pressuring EU countries to pay more for medicines to offset pharma revenue losses from lower U.S. drug prices. The U.K. is the only country to agree to pay more for medicines via a bilateral deal with the U.S.

Foundayo's arrival in the U.K. will initially provide competition in the private market. A decision on whether the National Health Service will cover the pill is not expected until Nov. 18, and will be made by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

World.title: Europe’s scorching summer is erasing its economic growth, says report
World.content:
The biggest drag is expected to come from people struggling to work in extreme heat. Triodos estimates lost labor productivity alone could shave around 0.6 percent off EU GDP, while agricultural output could fall by between 3 and 7 percent.

“At first sight this might seem modest, but it is exactly the expected economic growth for the EU this year,” said the bank of the overall €180 billion blow.

And the summer is not over. France and Britain are bracing for their fifth heat wave of the season this week, with temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius in southeastern France and 36 degrees forecast in the U.K.

The bill is already mounting beyond GDP. POLITICO estimated at least 14,000 excess deaths across the six hardest-hit European countries during the record-breaking heat wave from mid-June to early July.

Drought has also hammered Europe’s energy system: Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp cuts at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant and pushed Romania to blast apart a rock to divert water toward its last operating reactor. Vessels on the Rhine and Danube have had to sail only partially loaded.

In Austria, meanwhile, drought has caused an estimated €1 billion in agricultural losses, according to Austrian Hail Insurance, after some regions received more than 75 percent less rain than normal since mid-June.

Triodos warned against treating this summer as a freak event, saying extreme heat “might become structural” as the planet warms. But governments can soften the damage through irrigation, insulation, cooling and shifting working hours, said the bank.

“Every year adaptation without mitigation is a year borrowed against a hotter baseline.”

World.title: Moldovan president condemns Russia over killer drone crash
World.content:
Maia Sandu participates in a press conference in Warsaw on Jan. 26, 2026. | Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images

Chișinău has recalled its envoy to Moscow after two incidents in recent weeks.

Moldovan President Maia Sandu has blamed Russia’s war in Ukraine for a recent drone crash in the southeast of her country.

A drone crashed and exploded in the village of Crocmaz on Sunday, causing a fire that damaged several properties but caused no casualties. After conducting preliminary analysis on the fragments, local police said it could be a “missile-like drone.”

“I strongly condemn the latest violation of our airspace,” Sandu wrote on X, adding: “This is a direct consequence of Russia’s war, and it endangers us all.”

World.title: Farage demands sacking of Lowe aide as price of Reform-Restore talks
World.content:
On Monday the prospect of the two warring factions signing a make-up pact seemed to be at an impasse.

Farage used a press conference in Westminster to publicly state a new condition for holding discussions with “that party,” as he referred to Restore. Lowe must, he said, kick out Restore’s co-founder — a move Lowe has already rejected.

“I’m always happy to meet people and talk to people — within reason,” Farage said when asked by POLITICO what his conditions for entering talks with Lowe would be.

Leader of Restore Britain Rupert Lowe speaks to the media in Wigan, England on June 18, 2026. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images

“But I do think it’s fair to say that there are one or two people in the orbit of the upper echelons of that party who, if I sat down and talked to, I think our members and our voters would be utterly shocked that I’d done it,” he added.

“So we can talk to Rupert Lowe — that’s fine. But when you have co-founders, etcetera, putting out what I would call the ‘old theory’ — the old theory that we probably haven’t heard in this country since 1936 — and you have other adjacent publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country, just as an example…

“So the condition I would put on it is those people would have to be out of the inner circle — and I think that for me would be the only way we could sensibly proceed.”

World.title: Meloni, Frederiksen unite to condemn ‘uncontrolled immigration’ after Ceuta crisis
World.content:
In response to the Ceuta crisis, which reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration, Denmark and Italy had sent a joint letter to the European Commission demanding immediate action at the EU’s external borders. The letter was co-signed by 20 other European heads of state and government.

Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, with Rome announcing border controls for travelers arriving from Spain on Friday.

Meloni and Frederiksen argued that the adverse effects of illegal migration — “rising crime rates, growing pressure on public services, and an erosion of citizens’ trust” — were indisputable.

“For too long, ordinary people … have paid too high a price because of uncontrolled immigration,” they said.

“We are both proud of Europe’s Christian cultural heritage and want to protect it. We expect those who come to our countries and choose to make Europe their home to respect our values and not seek to impose ways of life on us that we do not share,” they said.

World.title: EU conservative chief demands migrant return hubs in Africa
World.content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her right-wing government are among the harshest critics, with Rome introducing border controls for travelers from Spain on Friday and sparking retaliation from Madrid.

Weber echoed proposals made last week by EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner, arguing that countries outside the bloc could be offered closer trade ties, economic collaboration and legal migration opportunities in exchange for accepting the installation of return hubs.

“Migrants who have no right to remain must leave Europe — no ifs, ands or buts!” he wrote, adding that returns must no longer depend on the political will of individual member countries.

Weber called for expanding the EU’s border and coast guard agency Frontex to 50,000 operational personnel, working alongside national forces and monitoring member countries’ compliance with the bloc’s border rules.

Weber also rejected internal border controls within Europe as a long-term solution. “They may be necessary in exceptional situations. But they do not address the root cause of the problem … There can therefore be only one answer: strong, joint European protection of the external border.”

In early June, the European Parliament and European Council announced new EU rules on migrant returns, including removals to countries outside the bloc in return hubs.

Weber also argued that the Ceuta crisis, which left around 100 dead, was the result of unilateral national action and said that the Spanish government’s “political signals” have had “an immediate impact on migration routes.”

World.title: What will Burnham do on AI?
World.content:
Artificial intelligence could transform the economy, the workplace, and even the way we think — but is Britain ready for it? And is Andy Burnham?

In the second of Sam Coates and Anne McElvoy’s summer box set conversations, they sit down with POLITICO UK tech editor Isobel Asher Hamilton to look at the choices facing the new prime minister this autumn.

Should Britain be building the next OpenAI, or focusing on using AI to revive manufacturing? Can the UK compete with the US and China? And where will the government land on the biggest political battles ahead, from copyright and data centres to the future of work?

World.title: Trump says will demand conflict compensation from Iran as part of peace talks
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday he would seek conflict compensation from Iran as part of any peace negotiations, citing attacks and killings stretching back decades allegedly backed or perpetrated by Tehran.

 

Negotiations on ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz have stalled and his new demands risk putting a quick agreement further out of reach.

Trump's announcement was a direct response to Iran's insistence that US payment of war reparations are a pre-condition to any resolution of the ongoing hostilities.

"I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran," he said, noting that his demand included not only damages arising from the current war, but also Iranian attacks on US targets going back more than two decades as well as payments to the families of Iranian protestors killed by authorities over the past 50 years.

In a later post, Trump also said that the Islamic republic should be responsible for deaths and damage it caused in Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza.

In what has become a regular pattern, Trump last week threatened to hit Iran "very hard," potentially with attacks against civilian infrastructure, only to pull back, hinting a peace deal was near.

A screenshot of a post on US President Donald Trump's Truth Social account, 10 August, 2026 @realDonaldTrump

Trump this weekend said he was "low-keying" his approach to the conflict, suggesting that he was prepared to let economic pressure mount in place of further military strikes.

Digital media outlet Axios said that the US president did not express any frustration with Iran's delaying an agreement to open the Strait of Hormuz in their interview with him published on Sunday.

Tehran has demanded that the US first end its blockade of Iranian ports and lift sanctions on its oil industry.

As negotiations have floundered, the strait's blockage by Iran has sent fuel prices soaring and rattled the world economy, putting pressure on Trump ahead of midterm elections in November.

In his post, Trump referenced the bombing of the USS Cole in 2000, which he has previously said Iran was "probably involved" in.

On Monday he said his various demands for compensations would be put "firmly into any, and all, future negotiations" with Iran.

Vehicles drive past a banner reading in English and Farsi, "We will kill Trump" in Tehran, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

Military shake-up

Meanwhile, Iran’s supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei named Revolutionary Guards general Ali Abdollahi head of the country's armed forces on Monday, while also confirming a new commander of the Guards, putting his imprimatur on the country's military.

Abdollahi had previously led the Khatam al-Anbiya, Iran's inter-branch central military command tasked with coordinating operations.

An statement on Khamenei's website announced that "Major General Ali Abdollahi has been appointed chief of staff of the armed forces. Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi has also been appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps with the rank of major general."

An Iranian pro-government demonstrator holds a poster of the Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in Tehran, 28 July, 2026 AP Photo

The pair represent Khamenei's first senior military appointments since being named supreme leader early in war after the death of his father in US-Israeli strikes.

Abdollahi has issued bellicose threats over the course of the war, warning regional neighbours earlier this month that "any country serving as a defensive shield for criminal and aggressive America will be engulfed by the flames of war."

World.title: Ceuta leader wants migrant detention centre after mass influx from Morocco
World.content:
The leader of Ceuta demanded on Monday the detention and expulsion of the thousands of migrants wandering the Spanish north African territory's streets after last month's mass influx from Morocco.

 

Some 72,000 migrants breached the border in an unprecedented and deadly rush between 30-31 July, with 70,000 having since returned to Morocco, according to Spanish government figures.

But the thousands who remain, including hundreds of unaccompanied children who cannot be summarily deported, struggle to access food, water, shelter and sanitation while the tiny enclave's resources are overwhelmed.

Their future has sparked a political battle between Spain's leftist central government and regions governed by the main conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox, which resist taking in unaccompanied children under existing legal provisions.

"A space that acts as an internment centre for foreigners must be set up, where these people can be held and remain confined," Ceuta's PP leader Juan Jesús Vivas told reporters.

Migrants who crossed into Spain from Morocco gather on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, 2 August, 2026 AP Photo

He said the measure "must be achieved urgently" so that the migrants "are not in our streets and that expulsion proceedings can be handled with greater speed and ease."

Vivas called the situation "unsustainable", estimating that between 8,000-11,000 migrants were left in Ceuta, well above the government's figure of around 2,500.

Thousands of residents of the territory of 84,000 inhabitants gathered to protest on Sunday at the handling of a crisis that they say has left Ceuta insecure and abandoned.

The Spanish government minister responsible for relations with the regions, Ángel Víctor Torres, assured Ceuta's population that police and troop numbers had been ramped up, including 40% more Civil Guards.

Reuniting the children with their families was "the priority," he added, without mentioning the possibility of expulsions.

Migrants who crossed into Spain from Morocco sleep on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, 3 August, 2026 AP Photo

Ceuta on alert amid fear of new mass crossing on 15 August

Ceuta is still trying to return to normal and authorities are preparing for the possibility of another attempted mass crossing. For several days, a call to cross the border from Morocco on 15 August has been circulating on social media, authorities to step up preventive measures.

Concerns about a possible repeat of what happened on 30 July have also led to extraordinary measures to ensure staff availability. The Civil Guard has temporarily suspended the granting of new leave, holidays and licences for officers stationed in Ceuta and Melilla, although the measure does not affect those that had already been authorised.

In parallel, the Ceuta Garrison has cancelled leave for military personnel stationed in the autonomous city from 13 August until further notice, except in exceptional cases.

The measures reflect the level of alert that remains in place at the border less than two weeks after an unprecedented influx. The authorities are now trying to prevent a new episode of migratory pressure from once again pushing the autonomous city's services and resources to the limit.
