The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", the prime minister said.

Experts urge caution over Hamas-Israel deal Middle East analysts are sceptical Hamas will willingly lay down its weapons and that Israel will totally withdraw from Gaza.

The suggestion the deal would allow Hamas to keep its weapons inside the strip, regardless of who was controlling or supervising them, was not a welcome development.

"Leaving Hamas with the ability to rearm themselves within a couple of minutes is extremely dangerous because at the end of the day Hamas has not changed," Yossi Kuperwasser, a brigadier general in the IDF reserves and the director of the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security, told the ABC.

"There's one point missing in these points of the new agreement. The first article of the [October 2025] 20-point plan was that Gaza is going to be de-radicalised. There's no reference to de-radicalisation here.

"So we are left with a radical Hamas governing Gaza and still very forceful, capable of re-arming itself.

"If we withdraw from Gaza under these conditions Hamas is going to be on the footstep, on the doorstep of the same villages and communities that it attacked on October 7th."

Hamas announced last month it had dissolved its emergency government in Gaza to allow NCAG to take over.

But Israel has described that as symbolic rather than anything of substance, accusing Hamas of keeping key officials in roles across Gaza's bureaucracy.

There was also an issue of sequencing since Hamas' statement suggested it would disarm once Israel had pulled back to the Yellow Line.

Israel, on the other hand, had long insisted it would only pull back once disarmament was completed.

Perhaps some of the debate there had come from Mr Trump's post on Truth Social, which said "as disarmament is completed, Israeli forces will withdraw".

Senior Israeli officials have also rejected the idea that the country had to stop its strikes on Gaza. They insist Hamas still poses a threat.

Since October 2025, when a truce was announced, Palestinian health authorities reported more than 1,200 people had been killed in Israeli strikes, among them many women and children.

Palestinians are in despair about whether Mr Trump's declaration will change much on the ground.

What does the US think of Israel's rejection?

Israel's rejection of the US-backed Board of Peace road map for postwar Gaza has reportedly left Washington unfazed.

A senior US official told Axios the White House "is not bothered" by Mr Netanyahu's statement on the Gaza plan and sees it as part of the election season in Israel.

"We understand Bibi's political needs. We have no problem with it as long as he continues to do what we ask — especially regarding restraining attacks in Gaza", the US official said.

How many weapons do Hamas still have?

Brigadier General Kuperwasser said assessments or estimates of Hamas' weapons stockpiles were not public this far into the war, which is quickly approaching its third anniversary.

"We assume that the number of heavy weapons, the rockets, is relatively small, but we don't know," he said.

"[The deal] refers to only some parts of the equipment of Hamas, the heavy weapons and mainly the rockets, which they have not used for ages now.

"So how do we know if they actually gave all of the rockets or not?"

In announcing it would disarm, Hamas revealed there were certain conditions that needed to be met by Israel. (Reuters: Hatem Khaled)

The issue of "personal weapons", like guns, is slightly different. The draft of the proposal said:

"Personal weapons in Gaza shall be subject to the provisions of relevant Palestinian laws. "The National Committee, as the transitional authority in Gaza, shall be the sole authority for registering weapons, issuing and revoking licenses, and enforcing the law, including through reintegration and social support."

Palestinians doubt Hamas weapons deal will hold Palestinians in Gaza have expressed scepticism about Hamas's declaration it will lay down its weapons in a bid to kickstart the stalled peace process, concerned it will not actually change the situation in the war-ravaged strip.

"I think the Israelis are saying something between 50,000 to 60,000 pieces of light weapons are still in Gaza, still in the hands of Hamas, other Palestinian factions, and also in the hands of families and clans in Gaza," Dr Abusada said.

"I think it's not going to be an easy task to go from door to door and collect all those light weapons.

"But let's also face it that these [are] light weapons, I don't think that they pose any threat to the Israeli side or any threat even to the communities next to the borders with Gaza."

Dr Abusada rejected the idea that this was a "new deal", as some in the Israeli establishment had quickly argued.

"It's the implementation of phase two of President Donald Trump's plan which was basically signed in October of 2025," he said.

What influence does the Israeli election have?

Both Brigadier General Kuperwasser and Dr Abusada said the upcoming Israeli election could have an effect on how quickly progress is made from this point.

It is currently scheduled to take place on October 27.

"I don't think this is going to be a contested issue in the election," Brigadier General Kuperwasser said.

"If Netanyahu is going to accept it he's going to be heavily criticised by his opponents. If anybody accepts [they are] going to be criticised.

"I think that the only people who are going to accept it are the Arab Lists and maybe the Democrats — maybe. I'm not even sure about that."

That likely means little movement prior to the end of October.

"We are not expecting that Netanyahu and coalition governments are going to … go smoothly with the implementation of this latest deal," Dr Abusada said.

"But at the end of the day I think most expect that maybe the next Israeli government, or the government that will be formed after Israeli elections, will have to carry out these understandings or this deal."

World.title: Will the RBA blink on inflation as the property market slows?
World.content:
Is this the beginning of the great unravelling?

Australian real estate and the glorified building societies that back it — sorry, our big banks — are on the turn.

And the blame is being sheeted squarely at the tax changes announced in the May budget, which wound back some of the excesses that had helped drive a 25-year property market boom.

Was it a bubble?

Quite possibly. At the very least it was on the cusp of fundamentally altering the structure of Australian society by creating a permanent class of landowners that would all but exclude anyone not born into it.

For years, a growing band of youthful would-be home owners were baying for change. That generational push was rapidly turning into a political force as waves of younger Australians became voters.

The aggrieved always make the most noise. And now the boot is on the other foot.

Those with property, who have sat idly by and watched real estate values climb to extraordinary levels, are upset by the prospect that the salad days are over.

Many had the quinella going: Go big on property and put the rest of your cash into shares in the banks which profited from fuelling the boom.

High interest rates are here to stay We seem to have flipped from worrying about rising house prices to worrying about falling house prices. Well, some of us have, anyway.

Despite all the alarm, and the lurid headlines dominating the financial press, the current downturn is still relatively modest by even recent standards, although it has the potential to become a significant event.

Deflating a property bubble takes quite some skill; something that has escaped almost every government or central bank that has ever attempted it.

Think Japan in the post-80s boom. Or China since 2019. And let's not forget America in 2007.

The RBA watches the cascade of economic effects from house price moves. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Betting on the house

When Michele Bullock steps up to the lectern today, you can expect a repeat of the same message that the Reserve Bank of Australia has broadcast all year.

Inflation is the enemy. The RBA will do whatever it takes to defeat it, and the pain of higher interest rates is far more preferable than the long-term pain of entrenched inflation.

Michele Bullock will likely stay on message about the RBA's inflation focus. (ABC News: John Gunn)

When the RBA talks about inflation, it's talking about the cost of purchasing everyday goods like bread and butter and even petrol.

It is definitely not talking about the cost of keeping a roof over your head, unless of course, you are renting.

But those who own a home and are hocked to the eyeballs with a mortgage aren't counted.

Housing is only counted in the inflation figures if you are building a new one.

Loading...

As far as the RBA is concerned, real estate and the cost of a mortgage aren't consumer items, even though they have a huge impact on household budgets and spending.

So, publicly, the RBA has no interest in real estate prices.

Privately, however, each of the board members understands the enormous repercussions mortgage repayments and property price movements have on the economy, spending and inflation.

They're acutely aware that when real estate is soaring, wealthy home owners are more likely to borrow and spend on consumer items.

But if housing values drop too sharply, there can be a cascading effect on spending, investment and economic growth.

That's why you won't see a rate hike this month and, if this downturn continues, for the rest of this year.

Eggs and baskets

Westpac was under fire yesterday.

Australia's second-biggest housing lender, after the Commonwealth Bank, released some quarterly figures that highlighted the sudden downturn in its home lending business.

Home loan applications fell off the financing cliff, down 20 per cent.

Bank stocks have come off the boil as home loan applications fall. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Given home loans are the primary business of Australian banks, investors responded by sending Westpac's shares sharply lower, off more than 5 per cent.

It was more ammunition for the aggrieved housing industry in the wake of the federal budget changes that curtailed negative gearing for new dwellings and saw the 50 per cent capital gains discount replaced with an inflation discount.

The changes coincided with three consecutive rate hikes, and there's been an ongoing dispute among economists over which shift has had the biggest impact.

Going by Westpac's numbers, you'd have to conclude that, while both measures have caused potential buyers to hit the brakes, the interest rate hikes are the dominant factor.

While investor loan applications plummeted 26 per cent in the quarter, owner-occupier applications — which were not affected by the budget changes — fell 18 per cent.

If that 18 per cent drop was replicated over both sets of loans, the budget changes clearly have hurt, but by far less than the rate hikes.

The rate increases have had the greatest impact on the two biggest markets of Sydney and Melbourne, which makes sense given they were the biggest beneficiaries of the spectacular boom since 2023.

Nationally, prices have dropped 1.9 per cent in the past quarter. But the rate of decline is gathering pace, with even former runaway markets like Perth, Brisbane and Hobart either barely climbing or in reverse.

Sydney has now fallen more than 4 per cent in the past quarter. But that pales when compared with the pre-pandemic fall, the 20 months from mid-2017 to early 2019.

During that period, Sydney real estate dropped almost 14 per cent, and Melbourne shed close to 10 per cent. And this was at a time when interest rates were steady.

That downturn was deliberately engineered by the banking regulator, the Australian Prudential Regulatory Authority.

Concerned about the pace of growth in new lending, it deliberately targeted investors by placing restrictions on the banks.

If there is anything to learn from that period, it is that market dynamics can change swiftly and sentiment is fragile.

Loading

Lessons from abroad

For all the warnings and threats from the RBA over the evils of inflation, central banks have been reluctant to address runaway asset prices until it's too late.

Property market downturn deepens Australia's housing downturn is spreading across the country, with the latest property price data showing previously resilient markets that had recently set record-high prices are now experiencing a decline in values.

At the height of Japan's stupendous property boom in the 80s, the couple of hectares that housed the Imperial Palace was valued at about $US5.1 trillion, worth more than all the real estate in California.

When the Bank of Japan popped the bubble with a punishing series of rate hikes, it took the Japanese economy with it, resulting in decades of recession from which it has never really recovered.

China's president, Xi Jinping, pulled the plug on its runaway real estate market just before the pandemic, wreaking havoc on the domestic economy ever since through weak consumption and investment.

Prices are still falling, forcing the country to rely increasingly upon exports, which is skewing global trade.

When the US property bubble burst in 2007, exposing malfeasance and reckless lending in the banking system, it almost brought the global economy to a halt.

Until now, Australian real estate has been among the world's most expensive, with Australians correspondingly among the world's most indebted.

Taking the steam out of the property market will be tricky, but entirely necessary.

And the RBA knows it.

World.title: Police mass AI surveillance pilot draws rebuke from privacy experts
World.content:
An Australian-first trial of live AI facial recognition technology by a police force has been criticised by privacy experts and legal advocates.

The mass AI surveillance pilot has been rolled out in Western Australia and is being closely watched by law enforcement agencies across the country.

Since the trial began in June, cameras linked to facial recognition software have scanned more than 130,000 people in Perth and Fremantle, comparing their faces against a police watchlist in real time.

Western Australian police say the results are promising but questions have been raised about an opaque watchlist and trial site locations that some say may target First Nations people.

The technology scans faces then compares them to a watchlist held by police in a van nearby. (Supplied)

In June, the Western Australian Police announced it would be the first police force to use live facial recognition technology on the public.

Facial recognition technology has become increasingly commonplace. It includes simpler one-to-one systems that check whether a single face matches a particular identity, like those used to unlock a mobile phone.

It also includes the more complex one-to-many systems like those used in Bunnings to compare faces of customers against a database of people suspected of activity including theft or abuse of staff.

Bunnings in breach of privacy laws, Commissioner finds The Privacy Commissioner finds Bunnings Warehouse interfered with the privacy of its customers by using facial recognition without consent in 63 of its stores over a three-year period.

Since June, WA Police have been trialling that more complex type of system.

Using tech company NEC's Neoface m40 product, a pilot program scanned more than 130,000 faces around Perth and Fremantle in the first week of the trial.

It compared their faces against a watchlist of about 4,000 people, including people accused of serious offences, people who are missing, and people who may pose a risk to themselves or others, police said.

WA Police celebrated the early results from the trial, which resulted in 33 alerts and 18 arrests.

Police say images of people not on the database will be deleted almost immediately and will appear pixelated, even for officers monitoring the technology. (ABC News: Callum Liddelow)

Of the faces scanned in the first week the algorithm falsely identified one person as being on the watchlist — a better result than the 2023 UK trial of the same technology.

Since then, the pilot has continued for several weeks across multiple sites, but WA Police declined to release any more data about the trial saying more would come in a "co-ordinated matter".

There are about 4,000 people on the police watchlist. (Supplied)

Technology has known accuracy issues, say experts

Melbourne Law School associate professor Jake Goldenfein said facial recognition technologies have known accuracy issues with particular demographic groups.

"Historically, these systems have performed worse for people of colour and for women, and especially worse for women of colour," he said.

That is because the algorithms used in the systems are trained on a data set of predominantly white and male faces, and an under-representation of other demographics in the training set results in worse accuracy.

Dr Goldenfein says facial recognition technologies have known accuracy issues. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

Dr Goldenfein said the systems produced both false positives, which could mean incorrectly identifying someone as being on the watchlist, as well as false negatives, which could lead the technology to fail to identify someone being sought.

When choosing the technology for its trial, WA Police pointed to the findings of a 2023 study by the UK's National Physical Laboratory which tested the NEC algorithm and found there were no statistically significant differences in false positives by gender or ethnicity when used under specific conditions.

But the study found accuracy issues increased when the facial recognition system's settings were relaxed and once real-world variables crept in, including changes to picture quality, lighting, skin tone and subject age.

WA Police are monitoring through screens located in a nearby van. (ABC News: Callum Liddelow)

Michael Birtwisle, an associate director of data and AI law and policy at the Ada Lovelace Institute in London, was called to give evidence at a 2023 UK parliamentary inquiry about the Metropolitan Police Service and South Wales Police's use of facial recognition technology.

He said Australian police could not rely on the UK's trial data when applying the technology here, particularly given the lack of testing on First Nations faces.

"It's a snapshot so it can only tell you [about] that version of that system, for that population," Mr Birtwisle told the ABC.

A UK study of the NEC algorithm found no statistically significant differences in false positives by gender or ethnicity. (Supplied)

WA Police did not respond to a question about whether NEC's technology had been tested or trained on First Nations faces prior to the trial.

"WA Police is committed to transparency and is collating statistics throughout the trial," a spokesperson said.

"The trial will assess demographics during the deployments and gauge whether or not there is a disproportionate impact on an ethnicity or group within the community."

Legal service left in the dark

Aboriginal Legal Service of Western Australia's (ALSWA) legal services director Peter Collins was on leave in June when he received an email from WA Police.

It was from a police superintendent asking for "20 minutes" to discuss the new pilot.

"This is the extent of the consultation: an email asking to meet two days before it is launched," Mr Collins said.

Mr Collins said he thought that WA Police would want the input of the state's primary legal agency for First Nations people involved in the trial, given WA's high incarceration rates of Aboriginal people and the risks of over-policing on a vulnerable cohort.

But he said the consultation was simply "an exercise in tokenism".

Mr Collins says police did not provide adequate consultation in the lead up to the trial. (ABC News: James Carmody)

"This was a done deal from the get go. No matter what ALSWA had to say about the pilot it would have gone ahead," he said.

Mr Collins said WA Police had not explained whether the technology was being used to identify children.

A WA Police spokesperson told the ABC that the force had made "attempts" to meet with ALSWA.

'Tick a box exercise'

WA Police completed an assessment of the trial's impact on privacy as part of its preparations.

On a form for the privacy impact assessment released publicly by police, it declared the trial would not "primarily or especially affect Aboriginal people".

Experts say there could be accuracy issues with the technology. (Supplied)

Peter Collins said the trial was one of the growing ways the WA Aboriginal community was being over-surveilled by police.

"It can only have been by design, not chance, that facial recognition technology has been rolled out in those suburbs and places where everyone is aware that significant numbers of Aboriginal people either live or frequent," he said.

"It is easy to understand why many Aboriginal people in WA believe they live in a police state."

A WA Police spokesperson said "the locations are identified ... based on policing need and policing objectives. Locations do not target any group of people or demographic."

Privacy expert at Electronic Frontiers, John Pane, said the consultation was thin but the bigger problem was the law that guides it.

"It grants extraordinary powers, with limited oversight, to a police agency to do incredibly invasive things," he said.

Mr Pane believes the privacy act needs to be amended urgently to keep up with the tech.

No consultation on trial, says watchdog

WA's privacy watchdog, the Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC), said the state police force did not invite it to take part in any "meaningful" consultation process for the trial.

The watchdog launched an unusually public broadside about the dangers of such a program without appropriate guardrails in July.

A WA Police spokesperson said it had briefed the OIC in April and invited the office to a demonstration of the technology.

WA Police have been displaying a sign letting the public know that live facial recognition is in use. (Supplied)

An OIC spokesperson told the ABC it turned down that invitation because it did not think it was appropriate to attend, given its role as an independent regulator and to avoid appearing as though it was endorsing the trial.

Former Australian Privacy Commissioner Malcolm Crompton said the Information Commissioner's missive was a clear warning from the agency.

"The police had messed up. They were caught, and I'll use the word caught," Mr Crompton said.

"And the Information Commissioner put a warning shot across their bows, very clearly."

Former Australian Privacy Commissioner Malcolm Crompton says the trial's privacy assessment was "feather-light". (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Mr Crompton, who now works as a privacy consultant, said the trial's privacy assessment was "feather-light" and should have undergone a proper consultation by an independent assessor.

"[The] privacy impact assessment is the cornerstone of this particular thing," he said.

"It's not an 'I'm going to wave this piece of paper in front of you and I've let you know it's happening consultation'," he said.

'It's going to catch more Aboriginal people'

Associate professor Hannah McGlade is a human rights lawyer and Noongar woman based at Curtin University in Perth.

She said she had deep concerns about the roll out of a program that would impact First Nations people more than other groups.

"This new policing program is looking at people with outstanding warrants. We know Aboriginal people are over-represented here," Dr McGlade said.

"The technology is being set up in well-known Aboriginal areas: Midland, Northbridge."

Dr Hannah McGlade says the program will impact First Nations people more than other groups. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

The human rights law expert said WA Police needed to be more transparent about who it had chosen to put on its watchlist.

"Should this sort of technology be used for people who have engaged in minor offending?" Dr McGlade said.

"Now, if people are at risk to the public, there might be other arguments in favour of it, or more surveillance. But here we just don't know."

Mr Birtwistle said the UK Home Office was currently considering laws that would limit inclusion on facial recognition watchlists to only those who had committed serious offences.

The ABC asked WA Police for more information on the nature of the 16 arrests for outstanding warrants in the first week of the trial. It did not respond.

WA Police say the trial's results have been promising, with 33 alerts and 18 arrests. (Supplied: WA Police)

Dr McGlade said the lack of transparency was unacceptable.

"And why aren't we being told? I think we're not being told because we will see that … Aboriginal people are being picked up more and over-represented," she said.

"If they've got nothing to hide then they really should show us who's being charged."

Dr Goldenfein said the WA trial could help shape how the technology was adopted elsewhere in Australia.

"I hope that as Australia starts to look again at the management of AI technologies in a more holistic way, the use of these technologies by law enforcement and intelligence apparatus doesn't escape that regulatory oversight," he said.

Other state police forces are paying close attention to the trial of the technology too, according to WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch.

He told a press conference when the WA trial was announced: "My colleagues, other police commissioners in other jurisdictions, are watching this trial closely to see how it goes."

World.title: First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCity life First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square Megan Gorrey August 11, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The City of Sydney is forging ahead with plans to bulldoze seven buildings opposite Town Hall to create a $150 million civic square featuring native trees and water fountains, new designs reveal, despite a backlash over the project’s cost and scale. Lord Mayor Clover Moore’s council in February voted to accelerate demolition of the buildings, including Woolworths supermarket, to make way for the long-promised public plaza at the corner of George, Park and Pitt streets in the heart of the central business district in about six years. An artist’s impression of the proposed civic square opposite Town Hall in Sydney’s CBD. Choi Render The designs include a curved grove of native trees and water fountains to cool the square. Choi Render Moore said the designs for the square, prepared by Sydney design practice JPW and landscape architects ASPECT Studios and to be published today, would mitigate rising urban heat.



“The trees and the water element will create a cooling environment for people to meet and greet or come to celebrations we might hold there,” Moore said. “I’m really thrilled that it’s very Sydney. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Clover’s vision: Town Hall Square will be George Street on steroids Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “It’s another change that will be fantastic for the city, and I think when people see it they will fall in love with it.” Moore said the 4200-square-metre plaza would feature eucalypts, moving water, seating and circular paving patterns to provide an outdoor venue for large events and celebrations including markets, festivals, concerts and sporting event live-sites. The square will have an Aboriginal name. “We’ve reached a point where we’ve acquired the buildings, we’ve saved the money, we’re ready to go.”



JPW director Matthew Morel said the “uniquely Sydney” square would “provide generous, flexible civic space found in the world’s great cities”. ASPECT Studios global design director Sacha Coles said night lighting would boost safety, and the square would be “a stage for Sydney’s civic life”. The City of Sydney has been planning for more than 40 years to demolish the Woolworths block and six other buildings to create a new public domain. The tree canopy would be lit up at night to improve safety. Choi Render The council hopes the square will provide a live-site for sporting matches. Choi Render In February, Moore signalled her ambition to start demolition work for the square – which had previously been delayed for another decade – before the council term ends in 2028.



Between 1985 and 2019, the council acquired six of the seven properties required for the project, starting with the Woolworths building on the corner of George and Park streets. Negotiations are under way for the council to compulsorily acquire the final building, home to a Foot Locker shoe store, on George Street. Related Article Opinion

City life Sydneysiders must shape their new Town Hall Square before it shapes them Carlo Ratti Architect and engineer Councillors endorsed the proposed scope of works for the project, allowing it to proceed to the next stage of concept design, planning approvals and construction. When the development application is submitted next month, there will be an opportunity for public comment on the draft designs. The Central Sydney Planning Committee will decide the application. The square is due to be completed in 2031. Labor councillor Yvonne Weldon has opposed the project due to its steep cost, telling a council meeting earlier this year the project was putting the organisation under “serious financial stress”, and the public plaza would “come at the cost of other projects and programs”.



“I’m all about improving and expanding our public spaces, but to me, this just doesn’t stack up.” Business Sydney executive director Paul Nicolaou, a staunch critic, has also warned the project would weaken the city’s economic core when it needed more investment and jobs. The Woolworths building is among seven blocks that will be bulldozed for the square. Edwina Pickles “The proposal would require the demolition of an active commercial building at significant cost, followed by the further expense of constructing and maintaining a new civic plaza. At a time when governments and cities face competing infrastructure, transport, housing and safety priorities, it is difficult to justify such expenditure, particularly when the city already has substantial public open space,” Nicolaou has said. The council says it has allocated $150 million for design, demolition and construction. All costs for the square, including those associated with the termination of existing leases and funds to acquire the final property, have been factored into long-term financial plans.



Moore said the council would need to invest more than $200 million to upgrade the existing buildings to modern office standards so they could be rented – a spend she said would be “crazy”. Related Article Climate crisis Dark roofs, no trees and black roads: The Sydney suburbs designed to get even hotter “It was the same when we pedestrianised George Street – [critics said] it was too costly, it shouldn’t happen,” she said. “Private investment in George Street [since then] has been $8 billion; we anticipate this square will be an enhancement for people wanting to visit, work and invest.” Woolworths has said the Town Hall outlet is its most visited supermarket nationally, drawing 6.5 million customers a year.



Tourism and Transport Forum chief executive Margy Osmond said the council’s “once-in-a-generation” project would create a landmark, attracting investment and visitors and potentially changing “the way people experience this part of the city”. World.title: If space is the true measure of cruising luxury, this is a winner
World.content:
★★★★ Reviews & adviceShip reviews If space is the true measure of cruising luxury, this is a winner Kate Armstrong August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Silversea Silver Moon Built 2020

2020 The cruise Busan to Tokyo (seven days of a 14-day itinerary) via Kanazawa, Aomori and Hakodate

Busan to Tokyo (seven days of a 14-day itinerary) via Kanazawa, Aomori and Hakodate Passengers 596

596 Crew 411

411 Decks eight passenger decks

eight passenger decks Length 212.8 metres Silver Moon is one of Silversea’s Classic ships. The Ship Mirroring her sister ship Silver Muse, Silver Moon is one of Silversea’s eight Classic ships. An additional four in the fleet are Expedition ships. Owned since 2018 by the Royal Caribbean Group, the brand has maintained a loyal following, as reflected by the many repeat clients on this trip.



Boarding 



The spaces The Panorama Lounge serves morning tea and coffee and later morphs into a cocktail venue. Silver Moon’s true strength is its spaces. There are many, and these distinct and welcoming areas ensure there’s no pressure for room. It’s easy to find your patch. The Dolce Vita, the heart of the ship, is home to both reception and the shore excursion desk (I love its pale turquoise velvet accents). The elegant Panorama Lounge serves morning tea and coffee before morphing into a cocktail venue, while the Observation Library has books and games tables. True to its name, the cosy Arts Cafe serves up an arty theme along with a decent cappuccino, specialty teas and pastries. A pool deck, jogging track and fitness centre cater to the active. Evening restaurants range from the 220-seater Atlantide to the delightfully intimate 32-seat venue Kaiseki. The Venetian Lounge is an inviting entertainment venue. The stateroom A curtain divides the bed and the sitting room in the neutral-hued Veranda Suite.



Our Deluxe Veranda Suite is very comfortable. The palette is neutral and the layout is perfect. A curtain divides the bed from the lounge area where there’s a decent-sized sofa with cushions and a throw blanket, plus a coffee table and a generous-sized desk with adjacent shelving. Floor-to-ceiling glass windows let in plenty of sun; heavy curtains block out nocturnal lights. The verandah has deck chairs and a table. The bathroom’s full-length bathtub is a bonus, and perfect for winding down after the busy day on shore. A walk-in robe’s ample storage helps you keep things shipshape. The food S.A.L.T. Kitchen restaurant on Silver Moon. With eight restaurants, Silver Moon offers everything from French dishes at La Dame, to pizza at Spaccanapoli, to Asian fare and an omakase menu at Kaiseki. The quality between venues can vary, however. The “classic” restaurant, Atlantide, is the most reliable in terms of consistency, even though it’s the largest option. Our standout favourite, and to our surprise the least frequented, is S.A.L.T. Kitchen. During this cruise, it prepares superb Japanese and Asian fusion dishes. (S.A.L.T. is Silversea’s “Sea And Land Taste” program that offers locally inspired menus and land-based culinary excursions). For sweet lovers, the gelati, made on board, are consistently excellent. The S.A.L.T. Bar’s cocktail staff shake up the scene, with martinis to gimlets and any challenge thrown their way. Don’t miss the Silver Moon cocktail. Wellness



With a full program, I don’t have time to try the Zagara Spa, but it offers a hair salon, a thermal suite, massage and medi-spa treatments (including Botox and fillers), plus several seaweed-based therapies. For an extra fee you can access a compact outdoor relaxation space with a small hydrotherapy pool (the area is “private”, but shared with others who’ve upgraded). The well-equipped fitness centre has plenty of room, light and ocean vistas. Entertainment S.A.L.T. Lab is the venue for hands-on cooking classes. Here, it’s less about the “cruisical” and more about a variety of performances, held in the Venetian Lounge where club chairs are arranged around small tables, or you can sit in tiered banquettes. The program ranges from traditional South Korean music to the final evening’s Motown-style production. Themed dances, such as the 1970s-focused Boogie Fever, light up the Panorama Lounge. A jazz duo channel Ella Fitzgerald and other melodies at Silver Note, an intimate New York-style jazz bar that also serves cocktails, while pianists perform at various locations around the ship. The insightful presentations about each port by on-board lecturer Evelyn Evans are a hit. Daily classes range from bridge to origami, but my choice is the class at S.A.L.T. Lab, a fabulous hands-on cooking session, where I learn to whip up grated turnip miso soup and daikon leaf rice. The crew



Although all suites have an assigned butler in addition to a room attendant, we have no requirements beyond the regular suite service and generally, the crew are pleasant and respectful. Service standards fluctuate in the restaurants, especially at breakfast, where there’s both a buffet and hot dish menu in La Terrazza. In smaller venues, it’s another matter; our server in S.A.L.T. Kitchen, Kai, describes each dish so evocatively that his enthusiasm alone makes it worth dining there. The verdict Subtle elegance, fascinating port stops and informative talks. The details Silversea’s 14-day (12-night) Japan itinerary sails from Tokyo to Tokyo. Fares from $19,100 a person. See silversea.com



Related Article Cruises Port guide: Tokyo, Japan Our rating out of five ★★★★ Swell An easy-going ship experience with attractive suites, refined and uncrowded spaces, an excellent choice of dining options and entertainment and a good selection of shore excursions (these may cost extra depending on the fare type).



Not so swell Standards: not Silversea’s fault (they consistently stress the dress code in communications), but some passengers insist on wearing inappropriately casual clothing in formal settings. And, as a non-smoker, I don’t appreciate how the designated smokers’ lounge (Connoisseur’s Corner) is located so close to the delightful Panorama Lounge. The writer was a guest of Silversea.

World.title: What happened to all the sex in The Odyssey?
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCinema What happened to all the sex in The Odyssey? Kerrie O'Brien August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Christopher Nolan’s interpretation of The Odyssey – the film that’s drawn millions to cinemas around the world since its release in July – is missing some of the poem’s really interesting women, and its sexiness, according to Classicist Mary Beard. “It’s de-feminised it,” she says. “And turned it into a kind of battle scene.” The UK-based writer, podcaster and former professor of Classics at Cambridge University is concerned people will walk away from the movie thinking that what Homer wrote in around the eighth century BC was an aggressive, tough story. “Actually, The Odyssey is one of the least macho works of ancient Greek literature,” she says. Calypso, played by Charlize Theron, appears in Christopher Nolan’s version of The Odyssey. But where’s all the sex? Alamy Stock Photo “I feel pretty strongly that this is an Odyssey rewritten for contemporary 21st-century American, slightly masculinist culture.” For Beard, one of the key themes of Odysseus’ homecoming to his wife is the rival sexual encounters on the way. “So there is Calypso, who keeps him as a kind of sex toy for about seven years and that is featured in the movie. But also you have Circe, this enticing witch, who – at least in the poem of The Odyssey – turns his men into pigs,” she says. “Now, the point of Circe in the poem is that she too is keeping Odysseus there to be her lover. Now, she’s not doing that in Nolan[’s film]; she’s a rather wonderful character ... but she’s not the same.”



Mary Beard says Circe (played by Samantha Morton) is “a rather wonderful character”, but she’s very different from the Circe Homer wrote. IMDB The film has entirely erased Princess Nausicaa, who lives with her parents on the island of Scheria. In the poem, says Beard, Nausicaa is just coming to marriageable age and is thinking about getting a husband when Odysseus washes up on her island, naked. There are these “quasi-erotic encounters” between them, she says. “They’ve downgraded the sex ... and so you’ve got a rather different feel to the whole thing. For me, The Odyssey is wonderfully domestic, wonderfully ironic. Sex is always at the margins – who’s going to entrap Odysseus next, or who is Odysseus going to decide to go off with next? And that has gone.” The Odyssey isn’t the only Nolan film to largely do away with sex. From Memento to The Dark Knight, most of the British director’s movies omit any kind of extended sexual encounter, earning him something of a reputation for creating “sexless” titles. One of the few outliers is Oppenheimer (2023), which contains brief scenes of partial nudity. The editor of Classics at The London Review of Books, Beard has made ancient Rome and the Classics her speciality over five decades. She points to the fact Homer’s poem was considered so female that in the 19th century, Samuel Butler wrote a book called The Authoress of the Odyssey claiming that it had to have been written by a woman.



Mary Beard has made ancient Rome and the Classics her speciality over five decades. Louie Douvis In Nolan’s take, Calypso (Charlize Theron) is the main woman other than Odysseus’ wife Penelope, played by Anne Hathaway, yet she appears in about 10 minutes of the three-hour film. Beard also argues that Nolan has introduced an entire theme that is absent from Homer’s original text, again perhaps inspired by our contemporary reality. “It is this sense we’re a civilisation on the brink of collapse, that there are threats coming to us ... Now, that is very much a contemporary American anxiety, a contemporary Western anxiety. In the original Odyssey, I don’t see a thing about civilisation coming to an end. Actually, it’s quite confident, [with] perhaps a misplaced confidence.” Anne Hathaway plays Penelope, wife of the long-lost Odysseus. Melinda Sue Gordon She is aware that the original poem is a lengthy beast and that Nolan had to make decisions about what would stay and what would go. “I’m not a pedant and these works are there for every age to do what they want with,” Beard says. “My job is to say maybe we’ve lost more than we’ve gained here. That’s all.



Related Article Literature The 3000-year-old poem Australians suddenly can’t get enough of “As the critiques have gone on and become rather more ferocious, I have become more sympathetic to him.” To Beard’s mind, The Odyssey is one of the most approachable works of ancient literature, “rich and complicated”. Recent interpretations include Caribbean writer Derek Walcott’s play of the same name and his poem Omeros, James Joyce’s novel Ulysses and the 2000 Coen Brothers film O Brother, Where Art Thou? The questions Homer asked are questions that we still ask, she says, so “there’s no surprise that The Odyssey has been so central in literature”. Regardless of her thoughts on his film, Beard does credit Nolan with inviting a whole new audience to discover this remarkable work, and for that she is grateful: “You’ve seen the film, now read the book.”



An evening with Mary Beard: Talking Classics tours Australia from November 20. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Of all the hotels I’ve stayed in around the world, this type is my favourite
World.content:
InspirationTravel tips Opinion Of all the hotels I’ve stayed in around the world, this type is my favourite Lee Tulloch Travel columnist August 11, 2026 — 5:00am

August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you asked me to name my favourite style of hotel, I would without hesitation say the Moroccan riad. A riad is a traditional Moorish house built around a central garden. In North Africa, particularly Morocco, it more often means a guesthouse in a heritage building where the rooms are arranged facing a shared courtyard. Some riads are quite simple, run by the family that has lived there for generations. Izza, Marrakesh’s central courtyard. The rooms can be small but even in the modest households, they open to courtyards covered in mosaic tiles, known as zellige, with a splashing fountain in the centre and surrounded by greenery, usually citrus trees planted in pots.



This style of inward-facing architecture that keeps families cool was perfected in the 12th century and little has changed. 



Apart from the astounding aesthetic beauty, there are many other things I love about staying in a Moroccan riad. Breakfasts are almost always included. Served with gallons of mint tea, they’re extravagant and dangerous for the waistline, especially msemen pancakes and baghrir crumpets, drizzled with honey. And I love the price. Staying in a riad can be surprisingly good value. Many will barely set you back $200 to $300, often less, in the centre of the city. Even more than this, I love the sense of place. The oldest houses are concentrated within the medina walls, which means guests are immersed in local culture as soon as they step outside the door.



Moroccans are extremely hospitable, so you’re not just invited into their house – you become part of their neighbourhood. But many riads fall into ruin because of the immense cost of labour-intensive repairs. The medinas of Marrakesh, Rabat, Essaouira and Fes have UNESCO World Heritage status. Increasingly, the houses in them are being bought and renovated by foreigners – it’s often only foreigners who have the money required to restore a heritage building. Riad Romeo, Marrakesh, owned by Italian fashion designer Romeo Gigli. Thankfully, many have been captivated by the magic of the medina. The restorations have sustained the skills of the traditional artisans, which might have been lost without private support.



Last year, I stayed at Riad Romeo, which is in one of the oldest parts of the Marrakesh medina. It’s owned by Italian fashion designer Romeo Gigli, who moved to Marrakesh when he retired from fashion more than 20 years ago. Gigli collaborated with local artisans on the traditional work such as the zellige tiling in the bathrooms and in the spectacular yellow-tiled waterfall in the courtyard, and on modern furnishings he designed himself. The result is a modern take on the riad that still retains many of the traditional features. Room Yves in Izza. The interiors are pink-toned and filled with vintage pieces. Izza and its art. Known as the “house of friends”, Izza was inspired by the bohemians of the 1970s who flocked to Marrakesh, such as Yves Saint Laurent, Talitha Getty and Marianne Faithfull, and the 14 rooms are named for each of them.



British tech entrepreneur Neil Hutchinson bought and restored eight interlinked riads, transforming them into one to create Izza and filling it with about €5 million ($8 million) worth of art from his collection. Izza is gorgeous, rambling across three courtyards and multiple rooftops, full of arresting art and contemporary furniture as well as magnificent zellige wherever the eye lands. Interiors at five-bedroom Riad Rosemary, Marrakech. Courtyard sanctuary in Riad Rosemary. Belgian artist Laurence Leenaert and her partner Ayoub Boualam opened Riad Rosemary the week of the 2023 Moroccan earthquake. The lovely five-bedroom riad is full of her bright ceramic plates and pots, which luckily mostly survived the upheaval.



Related Article Africa The unknown corner of North Africa that has been seen by billions Riad Botanica is owned by Angela and Mohamed Mallak (she’s from Melbourne; he’s from Morocco). It’s another small Marrakesh riad that has had a painstaking restoration and makeover. Traditional Moroccan mosaics, plasterwork and ornate cedar doors have been teamed with art deco wallpaper by Florence Broadhurst, an Australian contemporary twist. There are so many riads in Marrakesh, I could probably spend a year there and not stay in them all. Keep the mint tea warm for me. The writer was a guest of Riad Romeo and Izza.

World.title: Public transport is faster than the car in these 72 Brisbane suburbs
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic Transport Public transport is faster than the car in these 72 Brisbane suburbs Felicity Caldwell August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Living in the inner city isn’t always the best way to secure the quickest trip to the CBD on public transport. GoThere Brisbane analysis of 205 suburbs within 20 kilometres of Central Station discovered some outer locations such as Zillmere had faster public transport commutes than closer suburbs such as Coorparoo. The analysis looked whether a door-to-door commute into the CBD by 9am was faster on public transport or driving, and the number of routes and frequency within a 10-minute walk, measured from each suburb’s centre of population. A Brisbane journey planning website has compared travel times from more than 200 suburbs. Monique Westermann Among the best suburbs was Newstead, which had a 22-minute trip and 54 routes within a 10-minute walk.



Public transport beat the car in 72 suburbs, including Chelmer, Northgate, Zillmere, Taringa, Corinda, Strathpine, Graceville and Sherwood. On the other end of the spectrum, Upper Brookfield, in the outer west, had no practical public transport commute to the city, with no stops within a 10-minute walk. The nearest train was 11.4 kilometres away. In some inner-city suburbs, such as Paddington, Spring Hill and Annerley, a trip on public transport was comparable with a car journey in morning peak.



Franklin Smallwood, a student from Paddington, said he had great public transport options and several routes into the city. However, he said a car or bus trip often took about the same time. Franklin Smallwood lives in Paddington and says there are great public transport options into the Brisbane CBD compared with other suburbs. “The only issue with getting into the CBD is that during peak hours there will often be some completely full buses, but the frequency makes that not a major issue,” he said. The fastest door-to-door trips via public transport were from Bowen Hills, Fortitude Valley, Milton, Newmarket, South Brisbane, Taringa, Northgate and Wilston.



All the journeys from those suburbs were on a train, and they were all faster than a car. Despite the train being faster, only one in three suburbs had a train station within a 10-minute walk. In Brisbane, 58 per cent suburbs only had buses within a 10-minute walk and just five – the city, Spring Hill, Milton, South Brisbane and Newstead – had trains, buses and ferries. GoThere founder Stuart Crispe said he was a big believer in “letting the train take the strain”. “I really wanted to see how bus-reliant suburbs stacked up against rail lines, especially since I didn’t give bus options much thought the last time I moved,” he said.



“Data like this would have been genuinely useful to have back then.” Related Article Exclusive

Cars Where in Brisbane do people own the most cars? Search for your suburb Crispe said the biggest thing that stood out to him was how much dedicated corridors mattered compared with distance from the CBD. “Some suburbs much further out actually beat closer inner suburbs on travel time because they sit directly on express train lines or busway corridors,” he said. “Zillmere, for example, is around 14 kilometres out, but its direct train link gives it a huge advantage over suburbs that rely on the roads being clear.



“As road traffic gets worse, places with dedicated rail links like that could become increasingly attractive to commuters looking to bypass bus and car congestion altogether.” The analysis also found a quick commute does not always have to cost more in housing. The analysis found 72 suburbs have a faster city-bound journey on public transport than by car. Courtney Kruk Nundah was a 22-minute commute for a median rent of $670 a week, while New Farm cost $1200 for a 19-minute commute. Griffith University transport lecturer Dr Kelly Bertolaccini said traditional public transport with fixed routes and schedules worked best in areas of high density but in sparsely populated areas, authorities had to trade off direct routes versus accessible routes.



“Consider the difference between building a bus station in South Bank versus building a bus station in Fig Tree Pocket,” she said. “Thousands of people could live within walking distance of a stop in South Bank, meanwhile you would be lucky to find a stop location in Fig Tree Pocket within walking distance of 100 people. “To ensure that buses through lower-density areas service enough people to be viable, designers use additional stops and winding routes that provide greater access. “Unfortunately, these indirect routes plus the longer total distance from the CBD means these routes will inevitably be less efficient.” Bertolaccini said in southern Brisbane, along the busway, bus was generally faster than trains.



“Express buses can be as quick as trains, as long as they have separate lanes,” she said. “Local buses aren’t comparable because the reason they are slow has less to do with being caught in traffic and more to do with their winding routes. Related Article Roads Our worst roundabout has 12 entrances and exits, and is pitch black at night “Adding more stops to existing train corridors is also a great idea, but building entirely new train corridors would likely be cost prohibitively expensive.” Bertolaccini said Brisbane should also increase housing and development density in areas with established public transport to avoid creating more low-density suburbs where it was impossible to provide transport alternatives.



A Transport and Main Roads spokesman said the government worked with the Brisbane City Council to deliver the new bus network and Metro, and was delivering rail upgrades, including Cross River Rail, the train manufacturing program, European Train Control System and Logan and Gold Coast faster rail. “While public transport is already a highly competitive option for many Brisbane commuters, we recognise there are opportunities to further improve travel times and service availability for some communities,” he said. A council spokesman said its Metro and new bus network had made travel easier and faster, and said there was a 30 per cent increase in patronage since 50¢ fares were introduced. “Local governments collect just three cents in every tax dollar, which is why keeping our city moving requires investment from every level of government,” he said. World.title: Can mothers prevent passing on mental illness? This new study offers insight
World.content:
Exclusive LifestyleHealth & wellnessParenting Can mothers prevent passing on mental illness? This new study offers insight Sarah Berry August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

April Wilson wanted the cheat code – the one that ensured her future children wouldn’t inherit the mental illness that ran through her family “It’s not one of the genetic gifts that I would like to pass on,” says the 34-year-old from Melbourne’s east. April Wilson says the findings of a new study give her hope. Ruby Alexander. While pregnant with her first child in 2024, Wilson asked her psychologist what she could do to mitigate that possibility. She was told that the best way was to take care of her own mental health, and decided to stay on medication for an anxiety disorder. Issues such as anxiety and depression affect about one in five pregnant women (and one in 10 fathers), yet research indicates many are extremely reluctant to take antidepressant medication for fear of harming the fetus.



More than a decade ago, there was an information vacuum about what might prevent mental health issues from being passed on and the impact medication might have, says Professor Megan Galbally, director of the Centre for Women’s and Children’s Mental Health at Monash University. So Galbally began a longitudinal study to help women make informed choices and provide the sort of cheat sheet those like Wilson were after. For the study, newly published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology, researchers recruited 149 pregnant women with depression. Some had chosen to continue with antidepressant medication through their pregnancies while others discontinued. They followed the women and their offspring until the children were eight years old, finding: Untreated maternal depression in pregnancy was associated with double the odds of a child having an anxiety disorder at four years of age.

Treating pregnant women for depression led to a reduction in depression and anxiety in children at four years of age, and in girls, at eight years of age.

For eight-year-old boys, the main predictor of anxiety disorders was current maternal depression.

No major developmental differences were seen among children whose mothers were on antidepressants and those who were not.



The researchers also found that the markers of stress – based on cortisol levels in the placenta, in the mother’s hair after giving birth and in the child’s saliva at the age of one (when the child was put in a mild stress situation in which the mother briefly left the room) – could also predict the onset of anxiety later on, but only among the girls. Related Article Opinion

Parenting It was my most shameful moment as a parent. Now I’m seeing it play out all around me Sarah Berry Lifestyle Health Editor Some anxiety in children is normal and is distinguished from a disorder by the level of persistence and how much the symptoms impact a child’s ability to function. “Female infants who had higher cortisol reactivity at 12 months were more likely to the meet the criteria for an anxiety disorder at eight years of age, really regardless of the other factors,” says Galbally, who plans to look next at paternal factors that may affect risk. There may be different pathways for mental health issues in boys and girls, which may also help to explain why anxiety disorders are twice as common in women as men.



But Galbally emphasises the findings are still preliminary and more research needs to be done. Still, they demonstrate that treating depression and anxiety in mothers is an important step in reducing the risk of anxiety in children. Whether treatment involves medication is a discussion each individual should have with their doctor. Says Perinatal Anxiety & Depression Australia (PANDA) chief executive Julie Borninkhof: “It’s really important we take this information as golden because it gives us more insight. We want people to be setting themselves up for success. Your mental health is not a privilege, it is your life.” April Wilson remained on medication for an anxiety disorder throughout her pregnancy and made sure she was physically active and taking care of herself. Despite doing everything in her power to stay well, she suffered a severe mental health episode after her daughter Zoe was born nearly two years ago.



“I started to have dissociative periods where I would lose significant chunks of time, and couldn’t remember any conversations that I’d had,” she recalls. “And I was having a lot of suicidal ideation.” April Wilson. Ruby Alexander. It was an eight-month journey back to feeling mentally stable again. Today, she is doing “really well” and feels excited by the findings of the Monash study. They give her hope that the trajectory for Zoe is not inevitable. “The more proactive we can be before pregnancy and during pregnancy, the better we set up our children for success in not having to navigate the same challenges,” Wilson says. But it is not a perfect art, and there are many who struggle through their pregnancy and beyond.



Related Article Opinion

Parenting I lied about my kids’ screen time. But I don’t feel guilty about it Sarah Berry Lifestyle Health Editor Emily Henderson was diagnosed with generalised anxiety disorder at 19 and had tried medication but wasn’t convinced it was helping her. She experienced side effects coming off it, and had concerns about taking medication while trying for a baby so she decided against it. From the moment she became pregnant three years ago, the 24-year-old fretted about losing the baby and, later, about staying afloat financially. “I said I was OK when I wasn’t really OK.” Henderson, from Armidale in country NSW, white-knuckled through until her baby boy was born, and then fell apart. Sleep-deprived and struggling to breastfeed, she felt an impending doom every evening. She was also crying constantly and experienced the sudden onset of germophobia, which led her to sanitise so much she developed eczema.



Five weeks after their son was born, Henderson’s husband prompted her to contact a psychologist. “You feel horrible guilt during your pregnancy for being anxious,” says the teacher and psychology student, who wishes there was more support for new parents. “When it is time for us to hopefully try for our next little person, it just really re-emphasises ... the need to keep on top of physical activity, and self-care and seeking help earlier.” Borninkhof says women should not beat themselves up for going through difficult periods. Getting help at any stage can positively change the trajectory for both the parent and the child: “The beautiful thing about raising our children is that we have so many times and opportunities to influence their development and their wellbeing.” If you or anyone you know needs support call Lifeline 131 114, Beyond Blue 1300 224 636, or PANDA between 9am and 7.30pm on 1300 726 306. World.title: How WA’s top private schools are tackling bad behaviour – from parents
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAEducation How WA’s top private schools are tackling bad behaviour – from parents Holly Thompson August 11, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Western Australia’s biggest and most expensive private schools has a new way of combatting poor behaviour – but not from its students. And it is not alone, with the state’s peak independent schools body reporting behaviour from parents as a growing topic of conversation that schools are looking to address. Scotch College principal Alec O’Connell. Scotch College, in Perth’s western suburbs, requires parents to sign a charter when enrolling their children at the school, setting out the expected standards of respect, decency and courtesy. “To ensure the safety and wellbeing of all, and to protect the reputation of the college, the failure to operate within the intended spirit of the charter may lead to the headmaster or the Scotch College Council taking steps to address unacceptable behaviour, including terminating an enrolment contract,” it reads.



Principal Alec O’Connell said while families formally acknowledged the charter through the enrolment process, its principles applied to everyone who engaged with the college community – including students and visitors. He said while the majority already did the right thing, the charter was used “in conjunction with our conditions of enrolment” to outline clear expectations. “As headmaster, I have asked a couple of families to leave our community as it reached a point where they were clearly not aligned to our college and values,” he said. “It had reached a stage where their attitude towards our college was having a direct effect on the ability of us to support their son, and more importantly for our staff to be able to perform their duties.” O’Connell said the charter was not introduced in response to a particular incident or report, but the school had become “increasingly aware that schools more broadly were having to deal with disrespectful behaviour within their communities”.



“If someone falls short of the expectations outlined in the charter, the first step is usually to remind them of the standards we share and to work towards a respectful resolution,” he said. Editor's pick Property prices Two suburbs dominate the top 10 list of Perth’s most expensive streets “However, if someone repeatedly or deliberately decides they no longer agree with, or are unwilling to uphold, the expectations of the college community, then they may need to consider whether this is the right community for them.” O’Connell said during his tenure has principal, he didn’t believe expectations had fundamentally changed – but the way people communicated had. “Communication is now far more immediate and often digital. That can sometimes create a different tone or distance in interactions, particularly when people are communicating by email or online rather than face to face,” O’Connell said.



“Occasionally, this can lead to what people might describe as ‘keyboard warrior’ behaviour, where individuals need to be reminded that respect and courtesy apply just as much in digital communication as they do in person.” Families sending their children to Scotch College are also earning one of the highest median incomes in WA, and fees sit at almost $36,000 annually for year 7 to 12. For international students, that climbs to more than $50,000 and, when the cost of boarding is included, comes to $82,522. O’Connell said he did not believe the amount parents paid factored into the way they behaved. “High fees do not provide an imprimatur to act outside of any value construct. Paying fees does not alter the shared responsibility we all have to engage respectfully,” he said.



“It is also important to say that the charter is not designed to create an adversarial relationship between the college and families. It is not about punishment or control. “The charter exists to protect the quality of relationships across the college. It supports a culture where students, staff, families and the wider community can feel respected, supported and safe.” Association of Independent Schools of WA executive director Chris Massey said Scotch College was not alone, and other schools across the state, and nationally, were coming up with new ways to address the problem. “These charters help to define, for parents, staff, students and visitors, what respectful behaviour and appropriate communication looks like,” he said.



“This shared reference point means everyone can focus on what matters most – students’ learning, safety and wellbeing.” Related Article NAPLAN WA’s NAPLAN results for 2026 reveal ‘clearly concerning’ trend Massey said a spotlight had been shone on parent-teacher relationships recently, particularly given changes in technology had made it easier for parents to contact schools and teachers. “Parents are rightfully passionate about their children’s wellbeing and education. Schools welcome, and share, that passion,” he said. “Like any community, from time to time, there may be moments where behaviour or communication that falls outside of agreed expectations needs to be addressed.



“The emphasis for many schools is now making sure these are understood by everyone and are available to the entire schooling community so when complex issues arise, everyone is approaching the issue on the same playing field.” Last week, Catholic schools across the state introduced a new code of conduct which makes clear parents could face consequences, including being banned from the school grounds, as a result of poor behaviour. Catholic Education WA executive director Annette Morey said the code made it clear that certain behaviours were unacceptable, but that it reflected what most families already do instinctively. “Most parents will read this and recognise themselves in it, and that is rather the point,” she said. It outlined unacceptable behaviours such as aggressive language, demanding meetings without notice, entering classrooms uninvited, posting defamatory material online, or harassing staff through social media.



Clear processes are listed for addressing such situations, ranging from reminders to formal warnings, and restrictions on contact. Catholic School Parents WA executive director Siobhan Allen said families had welcomed the clarity. “Avoiding conflict in front of children is harder than it sounds, but it matters,” she said.

World.title: I ate my way across Spain and learned why messy floors are best
World.content:
Opinion I ate my way across Spain and learned why messy floors are best

I once travelled across Spain with a group of Spaniards. I’d have breakfast at 7am; they would come at 9am. Then 9.30am, then 10am, until one day the hotel breakfast finished before they even turned up. Lunch wouldn’t happen until 2 or 3pm, by which time I was catatonic with hunger. As for dinner, it was so late that I had to go out for dinner before I could go out for dinner.

But I got used to it. I’d stay up later at night (easy to do), and get up later in the morning, and soon I was quite happy heading out to dine at the requisite 9 or 10pm. There’s no point being in a different time zone to the rest of the people in the country.

Pintxos bar floors … if they’re too busy to clean up, they must be good. iStock

Besides, I soon learnt that the Spanish also stop for a mid-morning snack (known as almuerzo) and get together at 5pm (merienda) over a glass or a coffee. That helped a lot.

“It’s because the Spanish are so social,” says Ruben Lopez Mesa, a proudly Spanish-born chef based in Orange, NSW. “We like excuses to catch up with a mate or family, and talk about politics or soccer.”

World.title: First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWCity life First look at the divisive plans for Sydney’s $150m Town Hall square Megan Gorrey August 11, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The City of Sydney is forging ahead with plans to bulldoze seven buildings opposite Town Hall to create a $150 million civic square featuring native trees and water fountains, new designs reveal, despite a backlash over the project’s cost and scale. Lord Mayor Clover Moore’s council in February voted to accelerate demolition of the buildings, including Woolworths supermarket, to make way for the long-promised public plaza at the corner of George, Park and Pitt streets in the heart of the central business district in about six years. An artist’s impression of the proposed civic square opposite Town Hall in Sydney’s CBD. Choi Render The designs include a curved grove of native trees and water fountains to cool the square. Choi Render Moore said the designs for the square, prepared by Sydney design practice JPW and landscape architects ASPECT Studios and to be published today, would mitigate rising urban heat.



“The trees and the water element will create a cooling environment for people to meet and greet or come to celebrations we might hold there,” Moore said. “I’m really thrilled that it’s very Sydney. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Clover’s vision: Town Hall Square will be George Street on steroids Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author “It’s another change that will be fantastic for the city, and I think when people see it they will fall in love with it.” Moore said the 4200-square-metre plaza would feature eucalypts, moving water, seating and circular paving patterns to provide an outdoor venue for large events and celebrations including markets, festivals, concerts and sporting event live-sites. The square will have an Aboriginal name. “We’ve reached a point where we’ve acquired the buildings, we’ve saved the money, we’re ready to go.”



JPW director Matthew Morel said the “uniquely Sydney” square would “provide generous, flexible civic space found in the world’s great cities”. ASPECT Studios global design director Sacha Coles said night lighting would boost safety, and the square would be “a stage for Sydney’s civic life”. The City of Sydney has been planning for more than 40 years to demolish the Woolworths block and six other buildings to create a new public domain. The tree canopy would be lit up at night to improve safety. Choi Render The council hopes the square will provide a live-site for sporting matches. Choi Render In February, Moore signalled her ambition to start demolition work for the square – which had previously been delayed for another decade – before the council term ends in 2028.



Between 1985 and 2019, the council acquired six of the seven properties required for the project, starting with the Woolworths building on the corner of George and Park streets. Negotiations are under way for the council to compulsorily acquire the final building, home to a Foot Locker shoe store, on George Street. Related Article Opinion

City life Sydneysiders must shape their new Town Hall Square before it shapes them Carlo Ratti Architect and engineer Councillors endorsed the proposed scope of works for the project, allowing it to proceed to the next stage of concept design, planning approvals and construction. When the development application is submitted next month, there will be an opportunity for public comment on the draft designs. The Central Sydney Planning Committee will decide the application. The square is due to be completed in 2031. Labor councillor Yvonne Weldon has opposed the project due to its steep cost, telling a council meeting earlier this year the project was putting the organisation under “serious financial stress”, and the public plaza would “come at the cost of other projects and programs”.



“I’m all about improving and expanding our public spaces, but to me, this just doesn’t stack up.” Business Sydney executive director Paul Nicolaou, a staunch critic, has also warned the project would weaken the city’s economic core when it needed more investment and jobs. The Woolworths building is among seven blocks that will be bulldozed for the square. Edwina Pickles “The proposal would require the demolition of an active commercial building at significant cost, followed by the further expense of constructing and maintaining a new civic plaza. At a time when governments and cities face competing infrastructure, transport, housing and safety priorities, it is difficult to justify such expenditure, particularly when the city already has substantial public open space,” Nicolaou has said. The council says it has allocated $150 million for design, demolition and construction. All costs for the square, including those associated with the termination of existing leases and funds to acquire the final property, have been factored into long-term financial plans.



Moore said the council would need to invest more than $200 million to upgrade the existing buildings to modern office standards so they could be rented – a spend she said would be “crazy”. Related Article Climate crisis Dark roofs, no trees and black roads: The Sydney suburbs designed to get even hotter “It was the same when we pedestrianised George Street – [critics said] it was too costly, it shouldn’t happen,” she said. “Private investment in George Street [since then] has been $8 billion; we anticipate this square will be an enhancement for people wanting to visit, work and invest.” Woolworths has said the Town Hall outlet is its most visited supermarket nationally, drawing 6.5 million customers a year.



Tourism and Transport Forum chief executive Margy Osmond said the council’s “once-in-a-generation” project would create a landmark, attracting investment and visitors and potentially changing “the way people experience this part of the city”.
